Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday that he feared his US counterpart Donald Trump "will continue" lifitng sanctions on Russia. Zelensky's relationship with Trump deteriorated after the Washington eased sanctions on Moscow as part of a diesel-supply deal, despite Russia increasing strikes on Ukraine.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said Saturday that he feared the United States would lift more sanctions on Russia and that President Donald Trump's action only "rewards" Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin.
Trump heightened a battle with Zelensky on Friday when he signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions targeting Russia's energy revenues.
The decision came despite Russia increasing strikes on Ukraine in the fifth year of its war, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
Trump had already announced that he had agreed to a deal with Putin to allow exports of Russian diesel in exchange for the easing of sanctions, and Zelensky said he feared more concessions.
"Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the 'diesel deal' is just the first step," Zelensky told reporters.
He said he still "personally" hoped that Trump will do "everything in his power" to make Putin end the war but added: "You cannot achieve this by limiting Ukraine's responses to Russia for killing our people. And certainly not by lifting sanctions."
Ukraine said at least two people were killed in Russian air strikes on Saturday.
$80 billion in funding for Ukraine
Earlier on Friday, Zelensky urged EU leaders to keep financing Kyiv's fight with nearly $80 billion more next year, as he insisted he was standing up for his country amid the fresh row with US Trump.
Trump branded Kyiv's actions a "disgrace" and said it was easier to deal with Putin than Zelensky, after the Ukrainian leader ordered his forces to resume strikes on Russian refineries.

"I defend the interests of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people exclusively," Zelensky told journalists after talks with EU leaders in Brussels.
Asked if he was being made a scapegoat for Trump's domestic woes ahead of the US midterms, Zelensky just smiled.
"This is my answer," he said, after an extended pregnant pause.
The latest breakdown between Trump and Zelensky has fuelled fear that the US leader is siding with Moscow.
Those concerns have been heightened by disruptions to a critical US-provided satellite system that has hampered Ukraine's ability to counter Russia's intense bombardments.
Ukraine uses the Starshield system from Elon Musk's SpaceX for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones. It also uses SpaceX's parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, but not for offensive operations.
Tech billionaire Musk – though a virulent Zelensky critic – said his company was not behind the disruption and a US official denied any intervention by Trump.

"Has the speed been fully restored to what it was before? No. Is the speed being restored now? Yes," Zelensky said.
In his speech to EU leaders, Zelensky said that he believed that most Americans supported Ukraine's fight against Moscow's invasion.
"At the end of the day, the American people will have their say," he said.
70 billion-euro question
While he grapples with Trump, European leaders put on a show of unity with Zelensky.
"This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia's sanctions," European Council chief Antonio Costa said.
"Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure."
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that "the situation in Ukraine is currently truly dire, with numerous Russian attacks and a tense relationship between Ukraine and the US."
"It is crucial that we, as Europe, demonstrate our unconditional support for them today – and explore what additional steps we can take," he said.

But the EU leaders will need to find more than just words to keep Ukraine going.
Zelensky asked the bloc to provide more Patriot missiles to shoot down Russian missiles and come up with an extra €70 billion ($79 billion) in support next year to help Kyiv keep fighting.
"This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back."
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen confirmed that the figure of €70 billion "has to be covered" and urged partner countries to "step in" and help. Leaders told her commission to come up with a proposal for the financing.
French President Emmanuel Macron said Kyiv's backers will analyse the demand, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the EU will discuss it before the end of the year.
Macron also said Europe was "working hard to help Ukraine strengthen its ability to defend itself through satellite imagery and early-warning systems, which are much needed."
Frozen assets
The EU is currently paying out instalments of a €90 billion loan for Kyiv that was set to help cover funding to the end of 2027.
But the Ukrainian authorities have warned they will still face a major budget black hole as Russian strikes have battered the country's economy.
The talks on new funding have reignited calls for the European Union to tap around 200 billion euros in frozen Russian central bank assets to fund Ukraine.
"The frozen assets are there. That's what should be used for supporting Ukraine," said Latvian premier Andris Kulbergs.
But there seems little momentum on that front as Belgium, where most of the funds are held, remains opposed.

At least 1,500 troops from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Poland are expected to participate in military exercises in Poland in November, rehearsing the deployment of a multinational force to Ukraine following a potential ceasefire with Russia.
According to The Times on October 17, the exercises will focus on preparing European forces for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine as part of security arrangements intended to deter renewed Russian aggression.
The drills will test the movement of military personnel, coordination between national armed forces, and the delivery of essential supplies, including fuel and food. These logistical preparations are considered necessary for any future deployment of European troops to Ukrainian territory.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting confirmed that thousands of military personnel would take part in the exercises next month. Streeting said the training would help participating countries prepare to support Ukraine’s military training requirements and post-war reconstruction.
The planned exercises form part of the Coalition of the Willing initiative, which brings together countries working on potential security guarantees for Ukraine following a cessation of hostilities.
According to The Times, the training will bring multinational units together to practice operating alongside one another, with particular attention to the practical requirements of moving and sustaining troops across borders.
The coalition’s plans have developed through a series of discussions between Ukraine and its European partners over the possible deployment of an international security contingent.
In January 2026, Ukraine, the United Kingdom, and France signed a declaration of intent concerning the potential deployment of multinational forces following a peace agreement. The proposed mission would support Ukraine’s defense capabilities, military training, and long-term security.

articles.title: Did Trump Lift Russia Sanctions? What the October 16 Waiver Changes - Diplomacy and Law
articles.summary: Did Trump Lift Russia Sanctions? What the October 16 Waiver Changes  Diplomacy and Law
articles.full_text:
President Donald Trump did not lift the broader U.S. sanctions regime against Russia on October 16, 2026. His Russia sanctions waiver suspended major measures under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, including an additional 500% tariff on Russian goods and 100% tariffs on imports from countries meeting specified criteria for Russian energy purchases or sanctions evasion. The executive order waived these additional duties before they took effect, rather than removing tariffs that had already been collected (White House, 2026).
The decision also covered new restrictions concerning Russian financial institutions, investment, energy transactions, and sovereign debt. Not every provision was awaiting implementation: the Graham Act's prohibition on purchases of Russian sovereign debt by U.S. persons had already taken effect when the legislation was enacted on September 18. Earlier executive-order sanctions, including applicable asset freezes and financial prohibitions administered by the Office of Foreign Assets Control, remain enforceable. The Graham Act itself was neither repealed nor permanently terminated (United States Congress, 2026; White House, 2026).
The waiver came two days before the October 18 deadline for implementing the additional tariffs and contains no fixed expiration date. It remains effective until the President or Secretary of State, following the prescribed consultations, determines that further action is appropriate. For major purchasers of Russian energy, particularly China and India, and other significant importers such as Turkey, the decision suspends prospective American tariff pressure without establishing that any of these countries had been formally identified for the proposed 100% duties. It also limits the additional economic pressure Congress intended to impose on Moscow during Russia's continuing war against Ukraine.
The international legal consequences depend on the distinction between American sanctions, European Union restrictive measures, and sanctions imposed by the United Nations Security Council. EU restrictions operate under an independent legal framework, while binding Security Council measures derive their authority from the UN Charter. The Security Council has not established a comprehensive sanctions regime against Russia in response to its invasion of Ukraine, although individual Russian persons or entities may be subject to other UN sanctions regimes. Washington's October 16 decision cannot terminate European restrictions or alter independently binding Security Council obligations. Its legal effect remains confined to the American measures covered by the waiver.
1. What Did Trump's October 16 Waiver Suspend?
President Donald Trump's executive order of October 16, 2026, waived substantial sanctions and trade restrictions established under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. Enacted on September 18, the legislation introduced additional measures targeting Russian financial institutions, energy transactions, investment, and international trade. Section 115 authorized the President to waive specified obligations after submitting a national-interest certification and explanatory report to Congress (United States Congress, 2026).
Section 4 of the executive order exercises that authority across several provisions of the Act. The decision covers the proposed 500% tariff on Russian goods, additional 100% tariffs affecting qualifying third countries, and restrictions involving Russian financial and commercial activities. Although many measures were scheduled for implementation within 30 days of enactment, others had different commencement rules.
The order suspended the application of specified statutory measures without repealing the legislation. It also retained responsibilities for monitoring Russian energy purchases and sanctions evasion, allowing the administration to reconsider the waivers. The distinction is significant because the October 16 decision changed the immediate enforcement of the Graham Act while preserving the possibility of future action under its provisions (White House, 2026, Sections 3–4).
1.1 The Suspended 500% Tariff on Russian Imports
Section 112 of the Graham Act provided for an additional duty of up to 500% ad valorem on goods imported into the United States from Russia. Its coverage extended to merchandise generally, including energy products, subject to statutory exceptions. Section 2(a) of the October 16 executive order specified the 500% rate, but Section 4(a) simultaneously waived its application (United States Congress, 2026, Section 112; White House, 2026, Sections 2 and 4).
The proposed duty would have operated alongside other applicable customs charges. Its economic significance was the substantial additional cost it could have imposed on Russian merchandise entering the American market. However, the tariff was waived before implementation, and no additional duty was collected under the new measure.
The waiver does not eliminate earlier restrictions affecting Russian imports. Products prohibited under independent sanctions authorities remain subject to those prohibitions, while other applicable customs duties continue to operate. For Russian exporters, the October 16 decision removed a prospective additional trade barrier without restoring access to goods or transactions already restricted under American law.
1.2 The 100% Tariffs on Buyers of Russian Energy
Section 113 established a separate tariff mechanism intended to influence countries purchasing Russian energy or facilitating sanctions evasion. It authorized additional duties of up to 100% on goods imported into the United States from countries meeting specified criteria. The executive order selected that rate but waived its application before the new duties took effect (United States Congress, 2026, Section 113).
The initial statutory criteria distinguish two categories. The first concerns countries among the five largest importers, by volume, of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas during the relevant 12-month period preceding enactment, provided they knowingly make new purchases on or after October 18, 2026. The second concerns the five leading countries facilitating Russian oil-sanctions evasion during that reference period.
The legislation also contains exceptions and procedural requirements. Section 113(d) provides a limited exception concerning natural gas imports where the country's purchases account for less than 15% of Russia's annual natural gas exports during the relevant period and the country has taken significant steps to reduce those imports. Section 113(g) requires advance written justification to Congress explaining the tariff determination and the methodology used to identify the affected country. Subsequent country determinations are addressed separately under Section 113(e).
These conditions prevent a simple equation between purchasing Russian energy and becoming subject to the proposed tariffs. Country eligibility depends on statutory definitions, purchasing conduct, volume rankings, and the relevant exceptions. The October 16 order did not individually designate India, China, or Turkey as countries already subject to the additional 100% duties.
The proposed tariffs also differed from a direct tax on Russian oil purchases. They would have applied to covered merchandise imported into the United States from qualifying countries, potentially including products unrelated to energy. Their suspension consequently removed a prospective commercial penalty extending beyond the petroleum sector, while leaving existing American trade measures unaffected.
1.3 Other Graham Act Sanctions Covered by the Waiver
The October 16 waiver extended beyond customs duties. Section 4(c) suspended the application of specified sanctions and restrictions under Sections 102(a), 102(e), 103–111, and 117 of the Graham Act. These provisions addressed Russian officials, financial institutions, state-controlled enterprises, investment, financial transfers, securities transactions, energy activities, and international financial messaging services (White House, 2026, Section 4(c)).
Several restrictions were intended to limit Russia's access to foreign capital and commercial services. Others concerned American investment in Russia, transactions involving Russian government institutions, and activities supporting specified Russian energy operations. Their implementation depended on the particular statutory provision, including whether a prohibition operated directly or required an individual executive determination.
Section 109 provides an important exception to the general implementation chronology. It prohibited purchases of Russian government sovereign debt by U.S. persons upon enactment on September 18. The October 16 waiver subsequently included this provision. It would be inaccurate to describe every restriction covered by the presidential decision as having been waived before taking legal effect (United States Congress, 2026, Section 109).
The waiver also included Section 111, concerning Russian uranium, and Section 117, governing the termination of sanctions. The latter provision establishes a distinct legal procedure rather than another commercial prohibition. Its inclusion in the waiver does not establish that the conditions for permanent termination were satisfied.
The effect of Section 4(c) was to suspend substantial additional obligations under the Graham Act. It did not establish that every potential sanctions designation had already occurred, nor did it terminate restrictions created under separate American legislation or executive orders.

The deal additionally suggests expanding the 'Made in EU' initiative to encompass British manufacturers. Ongoing negotiations will be vital to garnering a unified stance among EU members and the European Parliament, with Britain's participation hinging on favorable alignment with EU trade and import regulations.
The European Commission proposed last year that CO2 emissions from cars should drop by 90 per cent from 2021 levels in 2035, but said automakers would have to close the gap to 100 per cent by using low-carbon steel and alternative fuels.
Under the Franco-German plan, the target would be set at 90 per cent without the need for any further compensatory measures. The softened target is broadly in line with the wishes of German automakers.
The joint plan also addresses an EU proposal that introduces local-content and low-carbon requirements for products bought through public procurement, public auctions or via subsidy schemes.
The provisional Franco-German plan says that for the automotive sector "Made in EU" should cover the EU's 27 countries and other European partners that were part of the EU internal market on January 1, 2020.
That would include Britain, which left the EU single market at the end of 2020.
An official at UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's Downing Street office said it would be good news for Britain's automotive sector if it was included in the "Made in EU" scheme. He said, however, that the Franco-German proposal would need European consensus and that details had yet to be seen.
The Franco-German plan also says that this inclusion should be subject to an agreement on full reciprocity, along with "dynamic alignment with EU conditions for investment from third countries and with EU trade protection measures".
That could mean Britain having to adopt the measures the EU has taken to limit imports of Chinese-built hybrid and battery electric vehicles.
Even with a Franco-German deal, the two countries still would need to convince other EU members and the European Parliament for their plans to enter into force.

articles.title: Exclusive: Romania president calls for NATO oversight in the Black Sea - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Exclusive: Romania president calls for NATO oversight in the Black Sea  Euronews.comPutin brings war into Nato’s waters  The TelegraphBulgarian PM summons Russian ambassador after ship sinks in Black Sea drone attack  BBCRussia's war reaches Bulgaria's shores, putting Radev's Moscow-friendly stance to the test  The Kyiv IndependentBulgaria Asks NATO for Aircraft, Air Defenses and Counter-Drone Systems as Black Sea Attacks Intensify  UNITED24 Medi...
articles.full_text:
In an interview with Euronews, Romanian President Nicușor Dan warns that Black Sea security is under growing pressure as drone attacks hit commercial vessels off Romania and Bulgaria.
Romanian President Nicușor Dan has said the Black Sea would only become safe after Russia’s war in Ukraine ends, as he called for greater NATO oversight in the region following drone strikes on commercial vessels in an interview with Euronews.
“I’m very optimistic that we’ll have the support and the capabilities in order to be better protected, because it’s an important economic question for Ukraine and for the whole region,” he said on the sidelines of an EU summit in Brussels held Friday.
The Romanian leader said frequent drone incursions into his country’s territory had begun roughly a year and a half ago, and that Bucharest had been “not prepared”. The country now faces a similar lack of preparedness to its east, Dan said.
“At the Black Sea, we are in the same situation,” he said, adding: “We have to protect the water under our territory.”
He also expressed confidence in continued support from US President Donald Trump, both for security in the Black Sea and for Romania’s position within the NATO military alliance.
“On defence, I think it’s a mutual benefit between us because we have an excellent position to project force towards other parts of the world,” Dan said.
The confidence comes amid bellicose statements from US President Donald Trump regarding Ukrainian and European security, such as troop cuts and a force posture review.
The president was in the Belgian capital for a quarterly summit attended by EU heads of state to discuss support for Ukraine, the bloc’s long-term budget and its growing trade deficit with China.
However, the increasingly hostile security situation in the Black Sea pushed the Romanian leader and his Bulgarian counterpart, Prime Minister Rumen Radev, to bring security threats higher up the agenda.
Dan told reporters after the summit that France had pledged “necessary equipment” and to “better understand our specific requirements in the Black Sea”.
“There are always new challenges, but fortunately, Romania has allies,” he said.
The escalating situation also prompted a meeting between the two leaders and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte to discuss stronger support. Bulgaria requested combat aircraft and anti-drone systems during the talks.
Rutte said afterwards that NATO would continue to strengthen its posture along the eastern flank, including by expanding its counter-drone capabilities.
“NATO will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed,” he said in a statement on the social media platform X.
Russia has repeatedly attacked Ukrainian ports along the Black Sea and the Danube River, leaving the war-torn country dependent on alternative routes to sell its grain to African and Middle Eastern markets.
However, this has exposed Europe’s shipping lanes to attacks.
Drones have damaged commercial vessels in the Black Sea off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania for three consecutive days leading up to the meeting in Brussels, as well as during the previous week. At least one vessel sank after being attacked by drones last week, killing two seafarers.
Neither Sofia nor Bucharest has definitively blamed Russia for the attacks. However, Radev told reporters earlier in the week that “logic” would suggest the Kremlin stood to benefit from the deadly incursions.
“The problem is that we cannot prove it,” he said.
Investigations into all the incidents are ongoing.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at a press conference after meeting European leaders on Thursday that “you do not need a ground war for an invasion to occur”.
He added that Russia was testing Europe’s response to the attacks, referring to incidents in the Black Sea as well as an explosive-laden drone found at an airport in Leipzig.
“Violating another country's airspace is already an incursion,” Zelenskyy said.
“We have seen drones cross airspace and borders in Romania, Poland and Germany. A corresponding drone was found in Germany, by the way. Moldova and Bulgaria have also been affected. A great deal is happening today.”
Zelenskyy and other senior Ukrainian officials have publicly blamed Russia for some of these incidents, most notably a deadly drone attack that struck a vessel carrying Ukrainian grain off the Bulgarian coast.

articles.title: Scotland must earn its NATO place, says SNP defence MP - UK Defence Journal
articles.summary: Scotland must earn its NATO place, says SNP defence MP  UK Defence Journal
articles.full_text:
EXCLUSIVE – An independent Scotland would hold the Greenland Iceland gap on NATO’s behalf and would have to demonstrate what it brings to the alliance beyond its geography, the SNP Westminster leader told me when I sat down with him to chat all things defence.
Dave Doogan, the member for Angus and Perthshire Glens, said his party’s policy of NATO membership carries obligations that cannot be assumed. “You can’t just want to be in NATO. You have to demonstrate that you’re worthy to be in NATO. NATO is a collective assurance and defence pact, and so if we are asking those current members of NATO to let us into that club, then we need to know, they need to know rather, that, well, what are you going to do over and above your geography, Scotland? And we need to be able to answer that question and answer it clearly.”
The geography itself would change name and meaning on independence, and Doogan set out what that would leave Scotland responsible for in the North Atlantic approaches: “If you look at an independent Scotland, the Greenland Iceland UK gap would then be the Greenland Iceland Scotland gap, and you and I both know that the corridor of principal tension between Russia and NATO is in that environment, that Euro-Atlantic region. So Scotland would have, working with their allies, a role in that.”
Doogan argued that Scottish membership would be an addition to the alliance and not a subtraction from it. “An independent Scotland within NATO makes the United Kingdom greater than the sum of its parts. There’s an additionality with an independent Scotland. We won’t be spending that five and a half billion annually, recurring and growing, on something else. We’ll be spending it on defence of the realm and defence of the Euro-Atlantic zone in cooperation with our allies, just like Denmark does, just like Norway does, just like Finland and Sweden do, and the UK do.”
He warned against treating the Typhoon force at Lossiemouth as a Scottish asset in all but name, arguing that the station exists for a job wider than Scotland: “Let’s not think for one minute Lossiemouth is there to defend Scotland alone. Lossiemouth is there to protect the UK’s northern flank.”
Doogan has already done the arithmetic behind that offer, having drafted and costed a plan for an independent Scotland with an army, a navy and an air force funded by around five and a half billion pounds a year. He wrote it about two and a half years ago, said it now needs updating, and corrected the suggestion that the work was unfinished, saying it simply needs a refresh. He is holding it back until the next independence referendum debate.
Asked why he has not published it, he said: “All of these things are about timing, and you know we can’t all see defence as a priority. I accept that, but actually, if we unpack these things, if we don’t have security, then we don’t have anything. And security isn’t just about territorial integrity and freedom of movement. It’s about food security, energy security, and a whole range of other things.”
He added that the document is written to answer a question that has not yet been asked in earnest: “Why not release the defence plan now? Well, a good reason is that it needs a refresh, but it’s designed to answer a question when enough people are asking that question, and that will come when we’re having the next independence referendum debate. Because I believe that it’s a cogent and sensible plan.”
Doogan described the document as “a signpost and a clarion acceptance that Scotland has a responsibility to defend itself as an independent state, and it has a responsibility to be a responsive and reliable partner to our allies.”
On the shape of the force, he said the plan assumes a conventional structure built up over a number of years: “The proposal that I’ve drafted and costed shows Scotland with a traditional three main service, army, navy and air force, and of course that needs generated over time. You don’t start with that, but you can have it on the drawing board.”
The budget comes from Scotland’s existing share of British defence spending, money he says is already being spent on Scotland’s behalf: “Scotland would be in a position to spend what it currently is exposed to in terms of the UK fiscal environment on defence, which is circa five, five and a half billion per share of the UK defence budget. That would be on a rolling year-on-year recurring with inflation, a budget that would generate a substantial defence force across three services.”
Doogan argued that the headline percentage tells you very little on its own, telling me “I often think two or three per cent of GDP is pretty abstract. Sometimes it’s not what you do, it’s the way that you do it. And the same is true, it’s not what you spend, it’s what you spend it on.”
He made the case for the naval component on industrial grounds, arguing that Scotland is among a small group of countries with the yards to build its own warships: “If you look at the amount of countries around the world that could have a stab at building a complex warship, there’s about twenty maybe at a push, and Scotland’s one of them. In fact, we’ve got two sites that can build complex warships on each side of the country.”
Doogan said he would be happy to go into where an independent Scotland would source combat aircraft, train its pilots and secure interoperability, while declining to treat those as prior conditions. “These are all legitimate operational questions, which I would quite like to answer, but I don’t feel the need to answer them because actually these are challenges that every sovereign state faces, and every sovereign state has to shop around for these platforms.”
On the division of existing British military equipment, he said the ownership position is clear but the practical answer is not. “It’s important to remember that we own the assets, all of them proportionately, at the disposal of the UK defence forces, and so we’ve got a call on them. But why would we make problems for the UK by taking our share?”
He set that against the state of the British inventory, where he argues the margin for giving anything away has long gone: “You know as well as I do that there is very little redundancy in any platform in the United Kingdom. You know, just look at what they were trying to do to get a functioning Type 45 out to the Mediterranean recently. If we think that there are squadrons of Typhoons up and down these islands ready to go at a moment’s notice, that’s not how it is.”
On that basis he ruled out pressing a claim that damaged what remained of the UK, telling me “So if we were to claim our share of eight per cent or whatever of UK assets, and that caused major difficulties for the UK, well, we just wouldn’t do it because it’s not intelligent.”
Division of assets has been one of the hardest parts of the independence argument to pin down since 2014, when the Scottish Government’s white paper assumed a share of equipment would transfer and the then British government declined to negotiate before a vote. The eight per cent figure Doogan uses reflects Scotland’s rough share of the British population, which was the basis the 2014 prospectus worked from.
On relations with what would remain of the United Kingdom, Doogan expects cooperation to follow from mutual interest. “Let’s not pretend for one minute that the United Kingdom, once all the heat has gone out of an independence debate and Scotland has chosen to be independent, the rest of the UK will cooperate with Scotland just in the same way it cooperates with every other entity and jurisdiction that used to be governed from London. It’s entirely predictable, because it’s to England’s and the rest of the UK’s self interest to cooperate with Scotland, and it’s in Scotland’s interest to cooperate with the rest of the UK.”
He added that the hostility between the two governments is a product of the constitutional argument itself: “This enmity that exists just now is a function of trying to keep the UK together. Once Scotland’s out of the UK, that enmity has no purpose anymore, and we’ll work together like grown-up and respectful states.”
Doogan said that losing jurisdiction over the northern half of the island would present the rest of the UK with a problem, and that he would not want it handled adversarially. “If the SNP or I have got anything to do with that, that won’t be a challenge because we’ll approach it in a cooperative way. How we do that is up for discussion. A brand new independent Scotland would not want to be undefended, but the rest of the UK would not wish a brand new independent Scotland to be undefended either.”
On the deterrent, he said Scotland would have no further say once the system left Scottish waters. “We have got no locus with the deterrent once it’s removed from Scottish waters. It’s not a Scottish asset or system, it’s a UK asset or system. And so what they choose to do with it, where they choose to berth it, whether they choose to sustain and renew it going forward into the future, that’s entirely up to the rest of the UK. Scotland will have no role in that. We’ll respect their sovereignty and their freedom of decision, and they’ll respect ours.”
Where the deterrent goes after independence would be settled in London, and Doogan accepts Scotland would have no say in it once the system leaves Scottish waters. The rest of the case is his to make, and it comes down to a navy and air force built around the North Atlantic, five and a half billion a year spent on conventional defence, and a neighbour the alliance can rely on. On his own test, that is what Scotland would have to show over and above its geography. He says he has the plan to prove it, and he is waiting for the moment to publish it.

articles.title: ‘Sleepwalking into Putin’s trap’: How Russia is waiting at the gates of Europe - The i Paper
articles.summary: ‘Sleepwalking into Putin’s trap’: How Russia is waiting at the gates of Europe  The i PaperNATO’s Top Commander Lays Out Plan to Thwart a Russian Attack on the Alliance  WSJNATO Details Plan to Shield Ukraine’s European Allies From Russia  The New York TimesRussia is at war with Nato ‘today’, says former top military commander  The IndependentNATO Has a Plan to Fend Off Russia. Now It Needs the Will  Bloomberg.com
articles.full_text:
Nato’s top commander issued a stark warning this week, saying that his troops will destroy “anything and everything” involved if a country was “foolish enough” to launch an attack on its territory.
“If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight,” US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich told the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday. “We will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those might be.”
Grynkewich’s blunt remarks came at a time of escalating tensions between Europe and Russia, with concerns that Moscow is preparing to expand its aggression beyond Ukraine, even by staging a limited military incursion to test Nato’s resolve.
On the front lines, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have for years warned of Moscow’s ambitions. But as the Kremlin escalates its aggression, and with Nato failing to deter it, the Baltics are increasingly worried Europe could be stumbling into a trap.
Russia’s brutal legacy in the Baltics
Artis Pabriks, a former defence minister and deputy prime minister of Latvia, told The i Paper that Russia has for years been using “strategic communications or cognitive warfare” within Nato to “depict the Baltic countries as something to which Russia might have more rights than it usually could have”.
Like much of Eastern Europe, the Baltic states endured decades of brutal Soviet occupation, until the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, an event Vladimir Putin has described as “the greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the century”. The Russian president has made reasserting Moscow’s dominance over former Soviet republics a core objective for his rule.
And Putin’s aims go beyond the control of foreign affairs and into direct influence over aspects of the internal policies of post-Soviet states, according to the Institute for the Study of War in Washington DC, which said that the Kremlin sees these countries as rightful parts of its sphere of influence.
“The Kremlin is working to split Nato,” said Edward Lucas, founder of the Baltic International Security Centre. “Specifically separating the Baltics and others including Poland from the rest of Europe, to deprive them of the protections of Nato and EU membership.”
The Baltics’ location bordering Russia means that they are more exposed than most Nato countries, and Nato’s reluctance so far to strongly confront Russia appears to be increasing the likelihood of greater aggression from Moscow.
“What worries many of us in the Baltic region is that we are sleepwalking into such a trap,” warned Pabriks.
The Baltic states are small: Estonia has a population of just 1.33 million, Latvia 1.9 million and Lithuania 2.79 million. Lithuania is also located between Russia’s exclave of Kaliningrad and its ally Belarus, with the Suwałki Gap to the south. This strategic 40-mile corridor links Kaliningrad to the rest of Russia via Belarus. In the event of a conflict, closure of the gap would cut off the three countries from land reinforcements.
Moscow preparing ‘something symbolic’
While an outright invasion has largely been dismissed, with Russia still tied down in Ukraine, Putin could still see the benefit of targeting the region as a way to undermine Nato.
The Baltics have “long been a focus of Russian military planning, information operations, cyber activities and other forms of hybrid pressure”, said Melita Phachulia of the Stockholm Centre for Research and Innovation Security.
And Moscow has plenty of options, she added. “A more likely scenario would be Russia testing Nato’s cohesion through limited or ambiguous actions that remain below the threshold of conventional war,” Phachulia said, adding that this might include more actions like the sabotage of undersea cables, GPS jamming, drone incursions or the “weaponisation” of migration.
Lithuania’s president, Gitanas Nausėda, said in July that Russia was planning potential attacks on critical infrastructure in the Baltics or Poland, while Latvian intelligence has said that Putin was considering more hybrid attacks designed to “send a signal: stop supporting Ukraine, or you will have your own problems”.
According to Lucas: “Russia could do something symbolic, and that’s what we’re seeing at the moment: Russian testing, attacking our decision-making. And that is our weak point… That’s a problem in Brussels, chiefly Berlin, London, Paris, and of course Washington DC.”
Could Russia weaponise an ‘internal threat’?
There are fears, however, that Nato’s reluctance to confront such incidents could encourage Putin to try a small-scale incursion. Reports suggested that CIA director John Ratcliffe flew to Moscow in August to try to warn Russia against further escalations, especially in the Baltics.
“It’s not necessarily that Putin plans to occupy Estonia or Latvia or Lithuania,” said Pabriks. “But for him, it’s important to have a case where he can show that Nato doesn’t react properly and it’s an empty shell. He could do something against some Nato member country which is close to their border, say to take 5 sq km….We give up our freedoms by centimetres and metres and kilometres. And one day we wake up and we are under their boot.”
In 2021, leaked documents from the Russian presidential administration revealed it was planning to maintain influence in the Baltics by funding pro-Russian groups.
Estonia and Latvia have the largest number of ethnic Russians in the EU as a proportion of their populations, and Moscow has tried to weaponise Russian speakers in the Baltics as part of efforts to complicate relations with their Western partners. Russia has also used this playbook elsewhere, including in Ukraine.
In the Baltics, anonymous Telegram channels and low-level agitation has worked to spread discontent over issues including campaigns to remove Soviet-era monuments and Latvia’s move to reduce Russian-language instructions in schools. However, there is little sign of serious discontent.
“Since 1991, Russia has never in any seriousness tried to foment separatism in the Baltic,” said Donatas Kupčiūnas, Baltic fellow at Cambridge University’s Centre for Geopolitics, with Moscow’s policies to minorities abroad “subsumed under broader strategic considerations”. He added that even Latvia’s recent language measures prompted “only lukewarm protests from Russia, because it has bigger problems to deal with”.
Meanwhile in Estonia, attachment to the Russian language has gone hand in hand with increased loyalty to Estonia, according to Institut Montaigne, a Paris-based think-tank. “There’s no sort of ‘minority’ in the Baltic hankering to be liberated from local rule and put under under rule of Moscow,” said Lucas.
‘We will respond with all the force we can find’
“Vulnerability should not be confused with weakness,” said Phachulia.
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have invested heavily in defence and resilience, taking a whole-of-society approach with conscription and massive reserve military forces. All are outsized defence spenders, at around 5 per cent of GDP, while a Baltic Defence Line of fortifications, bunkers and anti-tank obstacles now winds along their borders with Russia and Belarus.
The presence of “trip-wire” troops from across Nato – a UK-led battlegroup in Estonia, and another each in Latvia and Lithuania – as well as air policing and reinforced regional defence plans, further seek to underscore that “any attack on the Baltics is not an attack on the Baltics – it’s an attack on Nato”, said Lucas.
Right now, Russia knows it cannot win a war against Nato. However, by escalating sub-threshold attacks in places like the Baltics, it is hoping that it may not need to.
The Baltics have warned Nato allies that if it cannot establish deterrence or punish Russia for hostile actions, Putin will grow bolder. “Russia is not our problem,” Pabriks said, ironically. “Our problem is our allies, which for decades have not been listening to what we have been telling them. Russia is escalating, and it is escalating because the West did not choose to respond.”
“Pull yourselves together and start to act, because we all are in danger with this,” he said of Nato.

articles.title: EU AI Act Deadlines Moved: Credential Press Reissues 16 Exam and AI Act Books - EIN Presswire
articles.summary: EU AI Act Deadlines Moved: Credential Press Reissues 16 Exam and AI Act Books  EIN Presswire

New editions follow the Digital Omnibus dates, the AIGP Body of Knowledge 2.1 and PECB's multiple-choice ISO exams, for candidates and compliance teams.
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, entered into force on 27 July 2026. It moved the EU AI Act's high-risk rules to 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. The Regulation itself began applying generally on 2 August 2026.
The dates matter outside the EU too. The Act's scope does not follow corporate geography: a provider outside the EU can be fully in scope when it places an AI system on the EU market, and so can a provider or deployer outside the EU whose system's output is used in the Union.
"We would rather reissue our books than leave one candidate studying for an exam that no longer exists," said Sotiris Spyrou, founder of Credential Press. "Every edition prints the version it follows on its copyright page. If the version on the board's own site is different, the book is out of date, and a reader can check that in a minute."
What the new editions follow:
- AIGP Exam Guide and AIGP Practice Questions, for candidates sitting the IAPP's AI governance exam: Body of Knowledge and Exam Blueprint version 2.1, effective 2 February 2026, with the EU AI Act dates as the Omnibus set them.
- AI Governance Framework and AI Governance Worked Scenarios, for compliance, legal and risk teams preparing for the new deadlines: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as amended by the Omnibus. The handbook works through the Regulation in the order it creates obligations; the companion decides 24 situations against the Articles.
- ISO 42001 Lead Implementer Exam Guide and Practice Questions: PECB's Candidate Handbook version 1.5. The exam is 80 multiple-choice questions with three options each, and 48 of the 80 measure evaluation rather than recall.

Seven more titles were reissued alongside them, for the CISSP, CISM, CCSP, FRM Part I and ISO 45001 Lead Auditor exams.
On PECB's multiple-choice ISO exams, ISO 42001 and ISO 27001 included, the pass mark really is a percentage: 70% passes, which is 56 of 80 questions. ISC2, ISACA and the IAPP report scaled scores instead, and GARP publishes no pass mark at all. The board-by-board table of published pass marks, with the source and review date for every figure, is at credentialpress.com/pass-marks.

In an unusually blunt intervention, executives from the Japanese automotive giant told The Telegraph the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate was “not sustainable” and should be changed to reflect “real customer demand”.

articles.title: Euronews crew say they were encircled and robbed covering protests - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Euronews crew say they were encircled and robbed covering protests  Euronews.comFrance: violence against journalists during protests requires immediate sanctions and implementation of our post-mission recommendations  European Federation of Journalists
articles.full_text:
Euronews correspondents in Paris covering the protests reported being targeted by masked individuals on Saturday’s major nationwide demonstrations following calls on social media to target media outlets and professionals to prevent coverage.
Euronews’ crew was assaulted by looters and rioters in Paris near the Place de la Republique on Saturday as they were covering the ongoing joint major protests organised by the so-called ‘Yellow Vests’ and student-led groups.
The crew was headed to another location from Place de la Republique – where the protests were being staged.
Shortly into their journey, they were confronted by masked looters robbing the nearby Intermarché Express supermarket on 14 Place Jacques Bonsergent, which diverges from Place de la Republique, and filmed it.
“We were standing on Boulevard de Magenta, not far from a supermarket that was being looted by young people, young adults, teenagers. When they saw we were filming, they started hitting my cameraman and attempted to take his microphone and they encircled us,” said Estelle Nilsson-Julien, Euronews’ correspondent in Paris.
“They then pushed him against the wall and started hitting and punching him. They punched him in the face, but because he was wearing a gas mask, protective eyewear and a helmet, he was not seriously harmed."
"He managed to get away with just some bruises on his face," she added.
Our correspondent also noted that the looters stole their camera during the scuffles, which was eventually brought back by a group of youngsters who saw what was happening. The returned camera however did not have the SD card, and all footage recorded was lost.
Nilsson-Julien reported seeing things on fire in the area in the immediate vicinity of the supermarket, and loud police sirens.
“It is to be honest anarchy in the streets. There are many young people who seem like they are ready for a fight and looting going on. So, the calm protests of earlier today, at least in this area, are completely over,” she said.
Another Euronews correspondent, Valerie Gauriat, covering the protests at the Place de la Republique also reported a violent incident with a masked individual earlier while conducting an interview with a protester.
She noted that a protester slapped the back of her head and mumbled profane words as they walked past, denouncing media presence at the demonstrations.
The incidents come after certain groups on social media called on protesters to target media outlets and personnel, to prevent “the spread of misinformation” about the protests and reported violence.

articles.title: IMF forecasts 3.1% global growth in 2026, with eurozone at 1.1% - Yahoo Finance UK
articles.summary: IMF forecasts 3.1% global growth in 2026, with eurozone at 1.1%  Yahoo Finance UK
articles.full_text:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Tuesday has raised its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1%, citing resilience in advanced economies and increased AI investment.
However, growth will still slow from 3.5% in 2025, while high energy prices linked to the US–Iran war pose significant risks, particularly for low-income countries excluded from the AI-driven investment boom.
Meanwhile, economic growth in the eurozone will slow to 1.1% this year before a slight acceleration in 2027, the IMF said, due to persistently high energy costs and weak consumer confidence.
The 2026 forecast in the latest World Economic Outlook by the International Monetary Fund was a slight upgrade of 0.2 percentage points from its July report and follows 1.2% growth last year.
Although eurozone GDP growth rebounded to 2.6% in the second quarter of this year after zero growth in the first three months, the fund expects inflation risks to persist well into next year.
The Middle East conflict and Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine have sent oil and natural gas costs surging around the globe, a major threat to the eurozone and other economies that import most of their energy needs.
The IMF noted in particular that "gas inventories remain below seasonal norms in parts of Europe, leaving gas market conditions vulnerable to adverse weather ahead of the winter heating season".
Inflation is forecast at 3.1% this year and 2.8% next year, well above the European Central Bank's target of 2%.
That could require ECB interest rates that curb household spending and investment, with eurozone GDP expected to edge up to just 1.2% in 2027.
"Core inflation is expected to return to 2% only gradually," the fund said, in the eurozone by mid-2028 and in Britain by the end of 2027.
Growth in Germany, Europe's biggest economy, is expected to reach 1.3% this year, and Spain's GDP growth will remain strong at 2.5%.
But France's economy is seen expanding by just 0.4% this year, sharply below the 0.9% growth in 2025, with unemployment rising to 8.4% from last year's 7.7%.
For Britain, the IMF raised its growth forecast for this year to 1.3%, up 0.3 percentage points from July.
But UK growth is expected to slow to 1.2% next year "as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment."
Prolonged conflict in the Middle East could put additional pressure
The United States' war on Iran, launched in February, has plunged the Middle East into violence and driven global energy prices higher as a result of Tehran's retaliatory actions.

articles.title: Rare pink diamond goes on display in France 100 years after amateur heist - BBC
articles.summary: Rare pink diamond goes on display in France 100 years after amateur heist  BBCSee more headlines and perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
A rare pink diamond is going on display in France for the first time since it was stolen almost 100 years ago to the day - the last time it was shown to the public.
The nine-carat, pear-shaped gemstone known as the "Grand Condé" was pilfered in an overnight raid on the Château de Chantilly in October 1926 and concealed in a hollowed-out apple.
The diamond - one of few royal jewels to survive the French Revolution - was recovered a few weeks later when a hungry maid at the hotel in which the thieves were staying took a bite of the apple.
It will once again be on display in the Condé Museum at the Château de Chantilly until 3 January.
The museum's director Mathieu Deldicque said that while the apple story may sounds far-fetched, it was widely covered by newspapers at the time.
Deldicque has faced questions about whether the exhibition may be tempting fate, especially given the string of heists on European cultural institutions in the past 12 months, including the daring daylight robbery of jewellery from the Louvre museum in Paris.
While he declined to reveal to CNN how much the diamond was insured for, he noted that extensive academic study into the properties of the diamond had taken place to make it uniquely identifiable.
The results of this analysis, as well as previously unseen archive material about the gem's history and theft, form part of the exhibition, according to the museum.
Naturally occurring pink diamonds are exceptionally rare and often sell for tens of millions of dollars. The highest price ever fetched for one at auction was $71.2m (£53.6m) in 2017, according to Sotheby's.
The exact origins of the Grand Condé remain a mystery.
It was first mentioned in 1740 in an inventory of Louis Henri de Bourbon, Prince of Condé, drawn up following his death, the Château de Chantilly said.
It then became part of the collection of Queen Marie-Amélie of Bourbon-Sicily, the wife of French King Louis Philippe I, and then her son, Prince Henri of Orléans, the Duke of Aumale.
He bequeathed it to the Institut de France, which now owns the Château de Chantilly, 50km (31 miles) north of Paris, along with thousands of artworks and manuscripts which became the Musée Condé collection.

articles.title: No Ukraine aid and EU budget cuts: What does Le Pen mean for the EU? - Euronews.com
articles.summary: No Ukraine aid and EU budget cuts: What does Le Pen mean for the EU?  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
Le Pen is campaigning on a platform that would reshape France’s relationship with the EU ahead of the 2027 presidential election, potentially setting Paris on a collision course with Brussels with far-reaching implications.
Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, is seeking to become France’s next president on a hardline anti-EU platform, pledging to cut the country’s contributions to the EU budget and end funding for Ukraine.
On Ukraine, Le Pen has repeatedly pledged to end financial assistance. Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Wednesday, she said that if elected, France could only sustain funding for six months because of the “perilous” state of its public finances.
“This funding will stop, and it is a matter of honesty to tell [Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy] the truth,” she told Euronews.
Zelenskyy hit back in an interview with the Financial Times on Thursday. “The price to pay is not as high as the value of people’s lives,” he said. “That is why I think Ms Le Pen is not fully familiar with certain details.”
He added that, if Le Pen were elected president, she should have access to “the most powerful European system that works”, stressing that Ukraine’s battlefield experience could benefit European countries.
Le Pen has also called for an end to EU sanctions against Russia, while saying France could continue training Ukrainian troops and supplying military equipment to Kyiv.
Her comments signal that Le Pen is prepared to take a hardline stance, pledging to end French funding for Ukraine in a position similar to that of US President Donald Trump.
Her stance also contrasts sharply with that of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who is often compared to Le Pen but has advocated continued support for Kyiv.
Speaking in the Italian Senate on Wednesday ahead of an EU summit in Brussels, Meloni delivered a forceful defence of Ukraine’s right to self-defence.
“Supporting Ukraine is not an alternative to peace, it’s what makes it possible,” Meloni said. “The peace we want is one that is sustainable, just and also safeguards Europe and our interests.
“Therefore, the position of this government will not change: support for Ukraine, pressure on Russia and Euro-Atlantic unity.”
‘France’s support for Ukraine goes far beyond aid’
“France’s support for Ukraine goes far beyond aid alone. It is primarily diplomatic,” Elie Tenenbaum, director of the French Institute of International Relations’ Centre for Security Studies, told Euronews.
He highlighted France’s leading role in initiatives such as the Coalition of the Willing, launched alongside the United Kingdom, as well as other mechanisms that “help keep Ukraine afloat”.
These include the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan (USL), whose implementation and disbursement depend on the political backing of major countries, including France.
Tenenbaum stressed that cuts to EU-level funding would have a greater impact on Ukraine than a reduction in France’s bilateral aid.
“If France were not only to stop providing bilateral aid and contributing to the EU budget, but also to actively oppose these kinds of mechanisms, then the entire framework of European assistance to Ukraine would be put at risk.”
According to figures from the German think tank Kiel Institute, France has committed an estimated €27 billion to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. This includes €7.9 billion in bilateral aid and €19 billion through European mechanisms.
Germany remains Europe’s largest provider of aid to Ukraine in absolute terms, having pledged more than €50 billion since February 2022, well ahead of France, Italy and the Netherlands. Relative to GDP, however, Denmark and Estonia provide the highest levels of bilateral aid.
Cutting France’s contributions to the EU budget
With six months to go before France’s presidential election, Le Pen is campaigning on a platform centred on tighter immigration controls, greater national sovereignty and measures to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, as rising fuel prices fuel public discontent.
Her party has backed capping France’s net contribution to the EU budget at €5 billion a year, down from €8 billion, according to figures published by the French Senate. Such a move would mark a departure from recent years, during which France’s contributions have generally increased, despite annual fluctuations.
Under President Emmanuel Macron, France has backed a larger EU budget, unlike countries such as Germany, which favour tighter spending limits. Paris has also called for new EU own resources, meaning additional sources of revenue beyond member state contributions.
Although France is a net contributor to the EU budget, it also receives substantial funding for its farmers through the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).
“France stands out among the major contributors as it is the only one that has so far supported an ambitious EU budget,” Eulalia Rubio, a senior research fellow at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.
She said Le Pen’s proposals reflected a “lack of understanding” of EU institutions.
“Spending varies slightly every year, so you can’t say, ‘We’re only going to pay €5 billion every year from now on’,” she commented.
Rubio warned that if France overcame the legal obstacles to cutting its contributions, other member states would have to make up the shortfall. Such a prospect could prove particularly contentious given that France is the largest recipient of farming subsidies.
On Wednesday, France’s National Assembly rejected the National Rally’s proposal to unilaterally reduce the country’s contributions to the EU budget for 2027, instead backing the government’s planned level of funding.
Thierry Chopin, an adjunct professor of European studies at Sorbonne University, said a National Rally victory could mark a break with France’s traditional role as a driving force within the EU and with the “intellectual contributions championed by Paris” in recent years, which had gained traction in response to global events.
Chopin pointed to France’s role in promoting European sovereignty, strategic autonomy in defence and trade protection measures. However, he said France’s influence had waned during Macron’s second term as its economic credibility declined.
“This credibility was not particularly strong to begin with, but it has worsened given the country’s budgetary situation, public debt and the difficulties facing its public finances. And then, once again, there are political considerations, because the executive branch has been weakened,” he said.
EU budget for 2028-2034
Speaking to the Financial Times on Wednesday, Le Pen described efforts to reach an agreement on the EU’s 2028-2034 budget by the end of 2026 as "anti-democratic."
She accused the European Commission of undermining “democratic processes” by advancing the budget ahead of elections in France, Spain, Italy and Poland.
Ahead of the vote, Macron has moved to secure key positions, including at the central bank, by appointing allies. On Thursday, the French president told EU leaders during a closed-door meeting that Paris favours reaching a deal this year.
Beyond the timeline, Le Pen is also focused on the substance of the EU budget. Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, she said she hoped to “build new coalitions” with like-minded parties to challenge what she described as an anti-growth mindset in Brussels.
She also suggested that the European Central Bank (ECB), led by Christine Lagarde, should revise its mandate to give greater weight to economic growth. The ECB is independent and its primary mandate is to maintain price stability.
Experts told Euronews they are sceptical that member states would support another major overhaul of EU fiscal rules following the sweeping reform of the Stability and Growth Pact in 2024.
“In my view, member states show little appetite for another major reform,” Andreas Eisl, a senior research fellow in European economic policy at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.
He added that “future changes are likely to involve reinterpretations of the existing rules rather than a fundamental overhaul of their legal foundations”.
Le Pen has repeatedly criticised EU regulations and standards, describing them as “regulatory hell” or a “regulatory shantytown”, and has pledged to strip them back to the bare minimum. Such an approach could undermine the bloc’s legal framework if adopted across member states.
“Obviously, if every member state does this, the EU can no longer function as a union based on the rule of law,” Chopin said.
The National Rally leader has also vowed to “stop” the European Green Deal, the EU’s flagship programme to cut emissions and achieve climate neutrality by 2050.
Le Pen argues that the Green Deal undermines economic growth. She has also proposed abolishing institutions such as the European Committee of the Regions (CoR), an advisory body representing local and regional authorities involved in implementing EU policies, including climate measures.

articles.title: UK–EU “Switzerland Plus” Deal: Could Britain Return to the Single Market Without Rejoining? - Diplomacy and Law
articles.summary: UK–EU “Switzerland Plus” Deal: Could Britain Return to the Single Market Without Rejoining?  Diplomacy and Law
articles.full_text:
The United Kingdom could regain substantial access to the European Union's single market without rejoining the EU through a proposed “Switzerland Plus” deal. Such an arrangement could restore economic rights in selected sectors while leaving Britain outside the Union's political institutions. It would not automatically provide full single-market participation, and any additional rights would depend on the obligations negotiated with Brussels.
The proposal gained attention on October 15, 2026, when Bernd Lange, chair of the European Parliament's Committee on International Trade, suggested that Britain could develop a Swiss-style relationship with the EU, supplemented by closer political and strategic cooperation. His intervention followed Prime Minister Andy Burnham's call for a broader discussion about Britain's future relationship with Europe ahead of a UK–EU summit scheduled for November 20.
Switzerland provides an established precedent for substantial economic integration without EU membership. Yet its relationship with Brussels involves free movement of persons, regulatory commitments, financial contributions, and institutional obligations. For Britain, the central question is how much single-market access could be recovered through bilateral agreements and what legal and political concessions would be required.
1. What Is the Switzerland Plus Proposal?
“Switzerland Plus” describes a possible framework for closer UK–EU relations based on Switzerland's extensive bilateral agreements with the European Union. It is not an existing treaty, an agreed negotiating mandate, or a formal offer from Brussels. Its precise scope remains undefined.
Speaking at Europe House in London on October 15, Bernd Lange suggested a relationship involving economic agreements alongside cooperation on security, critical raw materials, digital policy, and other strategic interests. He also expressed support for Britain's eventual return to EU political decision-making, although he recognized that such a decision would belong to Britain.
Lange's position gives the suggestion political significance. As chair of the European Parliament's trade committee, he participates in the scrutiny of European trade agreements. He cannot independently authorize negotiations or commit the Union to a new treaty. Under Article 218 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), those responsibilities belong to the EU institutions exercising their respective treaty-making powers.
The proposed “Plus” element could extend beyond Switzerland's traditional sectoral economic arrangements. Cooperation on security and foreign policy, for example, could develop through separate political agreements without conferring additional internal-market rights. Lange suggested that negotiations might be completed within months following a British political decision, but this was an assessment of feasibility rather than an agreed timetable.
2. How Switzerland Participates in the EU Single Market
Switzerland is neither a member of the European Union nor a party to the European Economic Area (EEA) Agreement. After Swiss voters rejected EEA participation in December 1992, the country pursued economic integration through bilateral agreements covering specific sectors. This approach provided access to important areas of the European internal market while preserving Switzerland's status as a nonmember state.
The legal distinction is significant. The EEA extends much of the EU's internal-market legislation to Norway, Iceland, and Liechtenstein. Switzerland instead obtains rights through individual agreements defining the economic activities covered, applicable regulatory requirements, and institutional procedures.
Consequently, Switzerland does not participate in the entire single market on the same terms as EU member states. Its arrangements demonstrate that economic integration can extend well beyond an ordinary free trade agreement without conferring comprehensive internal-market rights.
2.1 The Bilateral Agreements and Their Limits
The first major package, Bilateral Agreements I, was signed in 1999. Its seven agreements addressed free movement of persons, technical barriers to trade, agriculture, public procurement, research, and transport. Bilateral Agreements II, signed in 2004, extended cooperation into additional fields, including Swiss participation in the Schengen and Dublin systems.
These agreements provide practical commercial advantages. The mutual recognition agreement reduces duplicate conformity assessments for covered products, while transport agreements facilitate access to European markets. The Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons grants qualifying Swiss and EU nationals reciprocal rights to live and work across borders. It also provides for the recognition of professional qualifications within its scope.
However, Switzerland remains outside the EU customs union. Customs declarations, rules of origin, and applicable border procedures continue to affect trade. Its agreements also do not provide comprehensive access to financial services or the full range of establishment rights available within the EU.
The original Bilaterals I package contains a further limitation. The agreements are linked through a termination mechanism commonly called the guillotine clause. Under this arrangement, termination of one linked agreement causes the others to cease applying. The mechanism reflects the EU's insistence that the concessions negotiated in 1999 form an interconnected package.
2.2 What the 2026 Bilaterals III Package Changes
Switzerland's bilateral relationship underwent substantial modernization through negotiations beginning in March 2024. The substantive negotiations concluded in December 2024, and the principal agreements were signed in Brussels on March 2, 2026. The Swiss Federal Council submitted the accompanying legislative package to Parliament on March 13.
Known as Bilaterals III, the package updates existing arrangements and establishes further cooperation concerning electricity, food safety, and health. It also introduces revised institutional provisions addressing regulatory alignment, supervision, and dispute settlement. These changes are designed to maintain consistent conditions in the sectors where Switzerland participates in the internal market.
A separate EU Programs Agreement was signed in November 2025, enabling Swiss participation in specified European programs, including arrangements applying retrospectively to research activities from January 2025.
The principal agreements signed in March 2026 remain subject to the applicable parliamentary and other approval procedures. Their signature did not bring every provision into force. The new institutional mechanisms, including those concerning dynamic regulatory alignment and arbitration, must consequently be distinguished from the arrangements already operating under Switzerland's existing bilateral agreements.
3. What Single-Market Access Could Britain Regain?
Britain's existing economic relationship with the EU is principally governed by the Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA). The agreement was provisionally applied from January 1, 2021, and formally entered into force on May 1. It provides preferential treatment for goods and establishes commitments covering services, investment, transport, energy, and other economic activities.
The TCA does not reproduce Britain's former participation in the internal market. British businesses operate as businesses from a third country, subject to the market-access rights granted by the agreement and applicable EU legislation.
A Swiss-inspired settlement could extend these rights in selected sectors. Its economic significance would depend on the obstacles removed. The distinction between tariff preferences, regulatory recognition, and unrestricted market participation is particularly important.
3.1 Goods Trade, Customs, and Border Controls
Under the TCA, goods meeting the relevant rules of origin can move between Britain and the EU without tariffs or quotas. Businesses nevertheless face customs requirements, product standards, and regulatory controls. The absence of tariffs does not eliminate the administrative obligations associated with trading across a customs and regulatory border.
A Switzerland Plus agreement could reduce some of these barriers through mutual recognition and closer regulatory alignment. For example, a British manufacturer exporting machinery to Germany could benefit if conformity assessments performed in Britain were recognized under an expanded agreement. This could eliminate duplicate testing for covered products, although customs procedures and other applicable requirements would remain.
Agricultural trade offers another possibility. A common sanitary and phytosanitary area could reduce veterinary certification and physical checks affecting food products. The UK and EU have already identified this as an area for negotiation. Such an arrangement would not, by itself, establish customs-union membership or remove every border formality.
Northern Ireland would require particular consideration. Under the Withdrawal Agreement, as modified by the Windsor Framework, specified EU goods rules continue to apply there. Closer regulatory alignment across Britain could reduce some trade frictions between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, but the existing legal arrangements would still require specific treatment.
3.2 Services, Financial Markets, and Establishment
Financial and professional services present greater difficulties because Switzerland's bilateral model does not provide comprehensive access to the EU services market. Switzerland does benefit from specific arrangements concerning professional qualifications and temporary service provision under its free-movement agreement, but these rights do not amount to general participation in the internal market for services.

articles.summary: EU eyes more financial support for Ukraine after US pivot  Financial TimesZelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace'  BBCZelensky and Europe cannot afford to go it alone  The TelegraphZelensky praises ‘real leaders’ in Europe as his relationship with Trump deteriorates  CNNEU’s support to Ukraine matters more than ever, von der Leyen says, as US relationship sours – as it happened  The Guardian

Your guide to what Trump’s second term means for Washington, business and the world
EU leaders on Friday vowed to maintain sanctions on Russia and discussed options to increase support for Ukraine after Washington signalled it would ease restrictions on Russian fuel to curb global diesel prices.
Leaders instructed the European Commission to draw up options to help Ukraine plug a financing gap estimated at €70bn for 2027 before the end of November, amid fears that Kyiv could run out of cash without additional funding.
“What additional financial needs we may have [for Ukraine] will become clear over the coming weeks,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said at an EU summit in Brussels. “I assume that we will have to address this again during [the next EU leaders’ summits in] November and December.”
Merz said it was still “open” whether the EU would raise debt to fund another loan to Ukraine similar to the €90bn agreed by the bloc last year.
“The gap that we see is in 2027, and it is €70bn,” Commission president Ursula von der Leyen told reporters after the summit, adding that the EU planned to shoulder two-thirds of that amount.
She told leaders inside the room that €21bn in unspent EU defence loans could be repurposed to finance weapons for Kyiv, according to people briefed on the discussions.
Other EU options to raise more cash for Ukraine could include borrowing against unspent funds in the bloc’s budget, or raising fresh debt from the markets, senior officials told the FT.
“We agreed that we need to address the additional needs,” said António Costa, European Council president, who chaired the talks.
Slovakia and Hungary asked to be exempt from any additional EU funding for Kyiv. Those two countries, plus the Czech Republic, secured an opt-out from the previous €90bn package.
Von der Leyen also said the EU was preparing a new round of sanctions against Russia, the 22nd package of restrictions since Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
European governments face a delicate balancing act as they seek to sustain financial and military support for Kyiv while easing domestic concerns over rising energy prices and the cost of living.
Donald Trump has blamed Ukraine for surging energy costs — a narrative that EU leaders are seeking to counter without alienating the US president.
Trump has eased pressure on Moscow in recent days in an effort to bring down fuel prices, while pressing Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. The surge in global energy prices, driven by the US war with Iran, is a major concern for the White House ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress.
Washington is to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel in a bid to lower prices — a move that has been criticised by Kyiv and other European capitals trying to maintain pressure on Putin to end his war.
The US is also considering lifting sanctions on some “shadow fleet” tankers linked to Russia to try to lower energy prices, and has floated unfreezing some of Moscow’s sovereign assets as part of efforts to revive peace talks with Ukraine.
But an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine declared by Trump last Sunday proved shortlived. After Russia continued to attack Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the FT in an interview that Kyiv was abandoning the truce.
Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU, told the FT when asked about the breakdown in relations between Trump and Zelenskyy: “That really just happened in the last couple of days . . . and so it really hasn’t affected anything yet.”
“If Europe wants to get it together and be supportive of Zelenskyy, we think that’s certainly their foreign policy decision. What we do in the United States may not always agree with that, but we’ve certainly been . . . supportive,” added Puzder, citing weapons sales, humanitarian assistance and direct military aid during the Biden administration.
Zelenskyy on Friday expressed gratitude for European support and said he was seeking to repair ties with Washington.
He said he raised the issue of Russia’s €210bn of assets frozen in the EU in his meetings in Brussels.
This included with Bart De Wever, the prime minister of Belgium, where most of the Russian assets are held. “The main thing is that Russia does not have the opportunity to influence, later on, these assets. Because we know very clearly that they want to bring these assets back,” Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy also said he was confident that Ukraine’s full access to SpaceX’s Starshield — the military version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet system — would be restored.
Kyiv was blindsided on Wednesday when Starshield began experiencing signal failures at speeds above 160kph, preventing the shooting down of Russian jet-powered drones.
Asked about European alternatives to the US system, Zelenskyy said: “We are not looking to completely replace Starlink. We are working with some countries, including France, to get additional capabilities.”
Zelenskyy said his country was still receiving US-made Patriot air-defence interceptors, acknowledging that Ukraine was competing for them with countries in the Middle East.
De Wever said earlier that he had told Zelenskyy the “financing needs of Ukraine need to be met and that, of course, a large portion of that will have to be resolved by [Europe]”.
However, there is growing fatigue among European leaders about the cost of supporting Kyiv.
Marine Le Pen, the far-right frontrunner in next year’s French presidential election, has said she would cut financial aid.
