articles.title: Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges? - The Guardian
articles.summary: Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?  The GuardianFridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack  BBCThe French fridge hack is a sign of the energy threats to come  The TelegraphCybercrims go beyond stealing data to attack physical building systems  The RegisterFridge hack costing millions and sparking fires stemmed from poor security  Ars Technica
articles.full_text:
Shortly before midnight last Sunday, the digital thermostats controlling hundreds of supermarket cold aisles across France began to flicker and rise.
In a “bizarre and unprecedented” cyber-attack, hackers had remotely overridden the temperature settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F).
Over the next four to six hours, the food inside first defrosted, then slowly began to cook.
Shop staff arriving early to restock shelves reported catching a blast of hot air, like opening an oven, when they went to fill freezers. One Normandy supermarket reported a number of its freezers had been pushed to 80C (176F). In certain stores, the extreme temperature rise had sparked fires triggering sprinklers and water damage.
“It was a catastrophe,” said one worker at the large Intermarché supermarket in the south-west suburb of Issy-les-Moulineaux in Paris. “They pushed the freezers here up to 62C. Everything had to be thrown away. It was such a waste.”
After removing tons of spoiled food, staff at the store worked until almost midnight on Monday to reorder and restock shelves. “Thankfully, we were able to get things almost back to normal the same day,” another shop worker added. “But we had to clear out everything in the freezers.”
If shop managers first assumed it was an isolated failure, it soon became clear up to 700 stores – including those from the Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains along with a number of smaller independent shops – had been victims of a cyber-attack.
Dominique Schelcher, the president of Coopérative U, said 80 of its 2,000 supermarkets had been targeted. “This is a completely unprecedented, unexpected, and extremely serious attack. In my entire professional career, I’ve never seen anything like it,” the shocked executive told French radio.
The Paris public prosecutor’s office immediately opened an investigation into the latest in a series of cyber-attacks that have made France the most hacked country in Europe.
Gérôme Billois, a partner in the cybersecurity and technology company Wavestone, said the hack had the hallmarks of political sabotage.
“The two most feasible scenarios are either it was a group of youngsters or activists who wanted to blow up a few freezers to prove what they could do, or it was a destabilising attack, what we call sabotage, by internal or external state actors,” he said.
“As for the attack’s signature, the most likely scenario is still a destabilisation attack – one designed to convey the message to populations that they are not safe, to convey the impression that the government is falling apart, and ultimately to instil fear.
“Currently there are two international actors known for doing this sort of thing: Iran and Russia.”
The hackers had pirated the controllers supplied by the Danish company Danfoss that controls the freezers and fridges. Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. Initial investigations suggest the hackers disabled alarm systems before tampering with the thermostats, or extended the defrost programme by several hours to avoid triggering alarms.
Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” that customers install updates or replace obsolete unsupported systems. The affected refrigeration units were “running outdated firmware”, it said. In the days following the first wave of attacks, France’s cyber-attack alert centre ANSSI confirmed supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted.
Marta Rybczyńska, a cybersecurity specialist and researcher, said she had found previous security warnings about old supermarket freezers running out-of-date software and newer models not having firmware updated.
“Some of these freezers hadn’t been supported by the manufacturers for several years and there were notices saying they should be replaced. Other freezers were newer but the software hadn’t been updated,” Rybczyńska said.
“The hackers found these weaknesses and used them.”
She added: “Many of the freezers appear to have been running with a default password. The hackers were able to modify or turn off the alerts so the shops only realised when the first person arrived in the morning and saw the damage that had been done.”
The most recent French cyber-attack mirrors a similar incident in the US in August when connected fridges and freezers at a dozen military commissaries – on-base food stores – went into unscheduled defrost cycles overnight causing massive food loss.
France is the most heavily pirated country in Europe by the volume of records exposed by hackers, according to the cybersecurity and risk management company Upguard.
In the last three years, hackers have breached France’s health system, France Travail, the government-run jobseekers agency, the National Agency for Identity Documents (ANTS) and most of the big mobile phone companies. This summer, the economy and finance ministry lost the personal and fiscal records of 678,000 taxpayers to a series of cyber-attacks.
Billois says France has fallen behind in addressing cybersecurity and has still not adopted the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act (2024) that introduced mandatory security for internet-connected devices.
“It’s a text that’s not political and that everyone agrees on but is delayed because there’s always more urgent legislation or there are quibbles about amendments, and this has been a disaster,” he said.
In the UK, the cyber security and resilience (network and information systems) bill to tackle cyber threats, is wending a similarly tortuous way through parliament. However, it fails to directly cover the food industry.
Supermarket boss Schelcher was quick to shift the blame for the attack on to unnamed refrigeration contractors who maintain the cold aisle equipment. “Our supermarkets are not customers of Danfoss,” he told RTL radio.
As yet, no individual or group has claimed responsibility for the supermarket cyber-attack; Paris prosecutors have instructed detectives from its anti-cybercrime unit but Billois says finding the hackers will take time.
“It’s possible they’ll be identified eventually, but it could take weeks if not months to be certain because hackers know how to hide their tracks,” Billois said.
Rybczyńska added: “Whether it’s possible to trace the hackers depends on their level of capability; if it’s a handful of youngsters, it’s easier because they probably won’t have thought to remove traces. If they are professionals it’s more complicated and will take longer. If they’re in a foreign country, it’ll be extremely difficult.”
The total cost of the cyber-attack has yet to be calculated but Thierry Cotillard, the CEO of Intermarché, said losses could run to “tens of millions of euros”, which store companies say is unlikely to be covered by their insurance.
“It’s a bizarre story,” Billois added. “There’s a shared responsibility between the supermarkets, the refrigeration companies who are sub-contractors and who maintain the material, and the software company. We cannot say who is to blame except, of course, the hackers.
“But in the end it comes down to freezers connected to the internet without being adequately secured. And that must be a wake-up call to everyone.”

articles.summary: Lagarde calls for fiscal discipline as energy inflation strains Europe  finchannel
articles.full_text:
The FINANCIAL — Christine Lagarde called for fiscal discipline on Saturday, Oct. 17, urging governments to keep energy relief temporary and focused on those who need it as Europe confronts renewed inflation and higher borrowing costs. The European Central Bank president said heavily indebted countries should restore room in their budgets through consolidation, revised spending priorities and more efficient public finances.
In her statement to the International Monetary and Financial Committee, Lagarde argued for a measured monetary response to an energy shock too large to ignore. She also said higher long-term interest rates would slow growth and limit the transmission of energy costs into other prices more than the ECB had projected in September.
The statement did not announce a new interest-rate decision. It set out the bank’s assessment of an economy facing pressure on prices alongside tighter financing conditions, with governments also being asked to preserve room to respond to future shocks.
Inflation rises across the euro area
The immediate inflation figures show the scale of the renewed pressure. Euro-area consumer prices were 3.8 percent higher in September than a year earlier, up from a 3.2 percent annual increase in August, according to Eurostat’s October 16 release. Prices increased 0.6 percent from August to September.
Energy prices rose 18.9 percent over the year, compared with 14.3 percent in August. Services inflation increased to 3.2 percent from 3 percent. The measure excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco rose to 2.5 percent from 2.4 percent.
The regional average conceals national differences. Annual inflation was 3.3 percent in Germany, 3.4 percent in France, 4.2 percent in Italy and 5 percent in Spain. A year earlier, euro-area inflation had been 2.2 percent. These are European harmonized consumer-price measures, covering a different geography from the United States’ consumer price index.
The ECB’s September rate increase
The ECB’s most recent policy action cited in Lagarde’s statement was a quarter-point increase in September. Its September 10 decision raised all three key rates by 25 basis points, taking effect on September 16. The deposit rate became 2.5 percent, the main refinancing rate 2.65 percent and the marginal lending rate 2.9 percent.
The decision retained the bank’s 2 percent medium-term inflation target and a meeting-by-meeting approach to policy. The ECB said it was not committing itself to a particular path for rates. Its assessment combines the inflation outlook and associated risks, underlying price dynamics and the transmission of monetary policy through the economy.
The bank also continued to let its asset-purchase portfolios decline by not reinvesting principal from maturing securities. It retained its Transmission Protection Instrument, which can address unwarranted, disorderly market movements that seriously threaten the transmission of monetary policy across euro-area countries.
Growth forecasts depend on a fading energy shock
The September ECB staff projections envisaged euro-area growth of 0.9 percent in 2026, 1.4 percent in 2027 and 1.5 percent in 2028. Those figures are forecasts, rather than completed annual growth results. The estimates for 2026 and 2027 had been raised by 0.1 and 0.2 percentage points, respectively, from the June projections.
Staff expected domestic demand to benefit from recovering real incomes and a resilient labor market as energy inflation eased. Infrastructure and defense spending, especially in Germany, and investment related to artificial intelligence were also expected to support activity over the projection period.
The export outlook was more qualified. Strengthening foreign demand was expected to help, but competitiveness problems would continue to constrain exports. The euro area was also expected to benefit less than some other economies from global AI demand because its AI goods sector is smaller.
Irish multinational activity adds another complication to the regional figures. A measure adjusting for that volatility put projected growth at 1.2 percent in both 2026 and 2027, followed by 1.4 percent in 2028.
The cost of protecting households
The International Monetary Fund’s October World Economic Outlook describes a global economy still expanding but facing an uneven recovery. It projects growth of 3.1 percent in 2026 and 3.4 percent in 2027, with global headline inflation at 4.7 percent and 4.1 percent, respectively. The estimates use information available through October 1.
Energy-importing economies outside technology supply chains face the most difficult outlook, the fund said. It identified further conflict, renewed trade tensions, fiscal vulnerabilities and a reassessment of AI expectations among the downside risks. Stronger AI investment and productivity gains, or sustained easing of geopolitical and trade tensions, could improve the outlook.
Its research on cost-of-living crises favors temporary, targeted income transfers that preserve price signals. Measures that suppress prices can require three to 22 times as many fiscal resources as targeted, temporary transfers, the report found. That range is a research finding across the episodes examined, rather than a fixed cost ratio for every government program.
Debt service narrows governments’ options
The IMF’s fiscal researchers have separately described the strain from higher sovereign borrowing costs. The average yield on 10-year government bonds across the Group of Seven rose by more than one percentage point between February and September, reaching its highest level in nearly two decades, according to an IMF fiscal-policy article published October 15.
The fund projects global public debt above 100 percent of global gross domestic product by 2030. It expects the effective average interest cost of government financing to rise from 2.3 percent in 2021 to 3.7 percent in 2031.
For the United States, the article projects interest payments increasing from about 2.8 percent of GDP before the pandemic to 5.7 percent in 2031. Those are projected future payments, rather than a statement of today’s federal interest bill.
Refinancing at shorter maturities can transmit higher policy rates to government budgets more quickly. The researchers also put the global primary deficit at about 3.3 percent of GDP in 2026, compared with roughly 2.6 percent needed to stabilize the debt ratio that year.
Financial markets retain vulnerabilities
The IMF’s October Global Financial Stability Report finds that markets have remained resilient, supported by growth and corporate earnings, while financial risks remain elevated. It identifies a possible correction in AI-related assets, a shock to sovereign bond yields and increasingly sophisticated cyber threats among potential triggers for turmoil.
The report describes the global banking system as broadly resilient, while acknowledging pockets of weaker banks. Among nonbank institutions, liquidity mismatches at insurers and pension funds and leverage in private credit could amplify stress.
Hedge funds hold about $13 trillion in assets globally, more than three times their 2013 level, according to the report. They can support liquidity and price discovery in normal markets. During stress, however, leveraged positions, crowded trades and correlated redemptions can force simultaneous asset sales, with losses or funding strains spreading to other institutions.
American technology finance draws scrutiny
The Reserve Bank of Australia’s October Financial Stability Review documents another connection between the AI boom and credit markets. Technology-related companies accounted for nearly 30 percent of U.S. investment-grade corporate bond issuance in the first half of 2026. That is a share of new issuance, rather than of all outstanding corporate debt.
AI firms are increasingly using corporate bonds, private credit, bank loans and asset-backed financing to fund large projects, the RBA said. It described aggregate leverage as contained and balance sheets as generally healthy, with large technology companies often supported by other revenue streams, including advertising and e-commerce.
Risks differ across the industry. Some data-center developers and cloud-infrastructure providers have weaker balance sheets or concentrated customer bases. Guarantees from larger companies and financing through special-purpose vehicles can support construction, while creating contingent exposures and links among developers, lenders and infrastructure investors. The RBA warned that opaque arrangements can make the industry’s financial exposures harder to assess.
Did euro-area prices fall in September?
No. Eurostat reported a 0.6 percent monthly increase and a 3.8 percent annual increase. A slower inflation rate would mean prices rising more slowly, rather than necessarily falling.

Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the Black Sea in the latest drone incident impacting the southeastern European nation, authorities said on Saturday.
Defence Minister Radu Miruta said the first drone had entered Romanian airspace at around 17:59 and was shot down "within two minutes," 25 km south-east of the town of Sulina.
"The second drone, in the same area, was engaged and shot down at 18:05, five minutes after entering national airspace, 20 km east of Sulina," Miruta said.
According to a Defence Ministry press release, two F-16s carrying out air policing missions were involved in the operation to intercept the drones after being scrambled from the 86th air base at Borcea, near the city of Fetești.
The aircraft were called into action after radar surveillance systems detected a number of aerial targets, per the ministry. It later announced that the targets were "jet-powered attack drones from the Geran family."
"The Black Sea serves as a critical maritime artery for the global export of grain, energy resources, and industrial commodities, making its stability vital to international food and energy security," Oana Toiu, Romania's foreign minister, wrote on X, adding that NATO would discuss Black Sea "defence and deterrence" at an upcoming meeting.
"The Black Sea will be safe again," she added.
Sitting on NATO's eastern flank, Romania is particularly vulnerable to security threats stemming from Russia's war in Ukraine, and the country has been dealing with a surge in drone-related incursions and incidents believed to be linked to the conflict in recent months.

articles.full_text:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Starlink speed limits are a ‘planned operation’
Simply sign up to the War in Ukraine myFT Digest -- delivered directly to your inbox.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that speed limits on Ukraine’s military Starlink systems were part of a “planned operation” aimed at undermining the country’s defences.
The Ukrainian leader’s latest comments come amid the sharpest deterioration in relations with US President Donald Trump since their explosive Oval Office meeting in February 2025, and as Moscow escalates its air war against Kyiv ahead of winter.
On Friday night, Trump refrained from imposing additional sanctions on Russia that were mandated by a sweeping law passed by Congress.
In a message to reporters over WhatsApp on Saturday, Zelenskyy said that Starlink terminals used by Ukrainian drone units worked at high speeds in the EU — up to 180kph — but cut out inside Ukraine when they flew faster than 160kph.
The maximum speed for Ukrainian drones equipped with Starlink systems was 161kph, he said, adding that “exceeding this limit causes the Starlink connection to cut out completely, resulting in the loss of the drone”.
He said Ukraine had conducted the tests to determine whether SpaceX was facing technical issues, as Kyiv had been told by Washington, or if the restrictions were a “planned operation . . . to restrict us, cut us off and prevent us from defending ourselves and protecting our people, both at the front and among the civilian population”.
Ukraine “sent a couple of vehicles equipped with Starlink terminals into European Union territory”, he said, without naming the countries where the tests were conducted.
“They moved at speeds exceeding 180kph, and the Starlink systems worked perfectly. We have the relevant logs and evidence to prove this,” he said.
“The conclusion is clear: the restrictions are in effect within Ukraine but do not apply within the European Union. In other words, this is a planned operation.”
Kyiv was blindsided by unexplained intelligence lapses from foreign partners about Russian ballistic missile strikes over the weekend, according to officials, which was followed by the surprise restrictions on Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet systems used by Ukraine’s military, particularly its drone units.
Ukrainian troops said they had been forced to suspend operations owing to the speed limits placed on the systems, which made them vulnerable to Russian air defences. Zelenskyy said on Saturday that the drone interceptors that Ukraine relies on to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones had also been hobbled.
He said Ukraine was increasingly relying on its fighter jets to intercept drones, with a success rate of more than 50 per cent.
Musk, who controls SpaceX, shifted any blame for the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield — the military-grade version of the system — to the Trump administration, noting that they were owned and controlled by the US government. He said any limits on speed or usage would have been decided by the Pentagon or the president.
Trump said on Friday that neither he nor Musk were responsible for the Starlink restrictions.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio reiterated that line to reporters on Saturday night. “No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it,” Rubio said. “But my understanding is it’s back up and running.”
A bipartisan group of senators on Thursday demanded the Pentagon open an investigation into the matter.
The intelligence gaps and the alleged throttling of Starlink came right before Trump waived new sanctions on Moscow.
Zelenskyy had praised the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which was signed by Trump last month, as a “major victory”. But on Saturday, he said “the lifting of sanctions will continue, unfortunately”. Zelenskyy added that Trump’s decision to exempt Russia “only helps the Russians”.
“It certainly doesn’t stop the war,” he said.
Last week, Trump also agreed with Russian President Vladimir Putin to “immediately” release 300,000 tonnes of Russian diesel to US and global markets ahead of midterm elections next month.
Zelenskyy also discussed with European countries information that Russia would attempt to reclaim frozen assets “through some partners”.
“But as of today the situation is under control,” the Ukrainian president said.
Kyiv was also surprised by Trump’s announcement last Sunday that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire”. Kyiv paused its own long-range attacks on Russian refineries for three days after the announcement, but resumed its campaign amid uninterrupted Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
“We’re done,” Zelenskyy told the FT.

articles.summary: 4 NFL arguments that fell off the grid after Ukraine destroyed that Russian bot farm  FanSidedUkraine targets Russia’s ‘Google’ as the internet becomes a new front line  CNNIs Zelensky right to say data centre strikes have taken down Russian bots?  BBCYandex outage: Data shows that instead of going dark, malicious bots went on the move  Cloudflare BlogDid Ukrainian strikes on Russian datacentres reduce online disinformation?  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
In the past week, Ukraine hit Russia with some kind of bombing attack, and it destroyed data centers that were apparently serving as some kind of bot farms. If there’s one thing that we can all agree on, it’s that Russian bots are real, and they’re programmed to sow discord in the most vulnerable areas of society. There’s a whole political side of that (I don’t do politics), but there’s most definitely a sports side of that.
On that sports side, those bots are definitely rooted deep in NFL Twitter. They could either be there purely to disrupt the reasonable status quo, or they could be there to learn about our culture as a football community. I’m not a scientist, so I don’t know.
My point is: if those data centers have gone down, that means the rats trying to stir up drama that makes everyone’s life terrible are gone, right? Yes, kind of. Maybe. Well, not completely. There are real people out there who have the same opinions, but a whole bunch of the bots are gone, and with that, we’ve seen some changes in online discourse.
Is any of this really because some villain headquarters got all blown up, or is it for some other reason? Your guess is as good as mine because we’re all equally dumb.
I’m not making any claims. All I’m doing is simply asking questions … That’s all. And these are some semi-reasonable, and possibly dumb, questions that have to be asked now that the propaganda machines have taken a hit.
What happened to the Tyreek Hill talk?
A couple of weeks ago, Tyquan Thornton went down with a gnarled-up ankle after he caught a mondo-sized pass from Patrick Mahomes in the fourth quarter against the Raiders. Kansas City has already needed help at the wide receiver position since the end of last season. With Thornton going out, it meant that they were also missing their field-stretching deep guy.
One of the bigger free-agent wide receivers out there is Tyreek Hill. There’s obviously a big connection between him and the Chiefs, so he was naturally being talked about as a guy that they would re-sign during their Week 5 bye … Despite him dislocating his knee last year, saying that he has “no power” in his leg three months ago and him being an all-around bad guy and psychopath. 
In other words, that’s the perfect type of player for a Russian Bot Farm to create a controversial conversation about. To be fair, that wasn’t hard to do … so they did.
There were a whole bunch of Twitter threads about how long it would take for him to get to the Chiefs and what that team would look like with him. Then, it just kind of stopped completely.
Is that because he’s in court right now? Or is that because the bot accounts that want a real-life villain back in the lives of the American public have been destroyed?
Why can’t the Eagles call plays?
The Eagles are one fanbase that doesn’t need international interference for there to be wild takes and propaganda thrown around. This is less about that than the other questions that I’ve been asking, and more about the actual mechanisms functioning in Nick Sirianni’s brain.
This offseason, Sirianni talked about how he discovered ChatGPT and how he used it to find motivational stories to keep his messaging to the team fresh. It was a dumb thing to say out loud, but to be fair, Sirianni isn’t exactly the smartest dude in the world.
There’s a non-zero chance that Sirianni just calls all AI platforms ChatGPT, and we know that he tries to get any kind of competitive advantage possible. That means there’s a non-zero chance that he used some kind of bootleg Russian-backed platform.
If that’s the case, would you be surprised if he asked this extranational entity for ideas on how to game plan? Would you be surprised if said entity realized that the head coach of a team with the most aggressive fanbase in American sports was asking for help? Would you be surprised if said entity gave Sirianni bad advice?
Then, the data centers go kaput, Sirianni doesn’t have a Grima Wormtongue in his ear, and the Eagles offense has a chance to do something … Unfortunately, all of the offensive playmakers are hurt, so things never ended up looking any better.
Where did the Deshaun Watson defenders go?
One of the most polarizing people in the NFL is Deshaun Watson; his past is sordid, at its very best.
Two weeks ago, something really bizarre happened: the Amazon broadcast on Thursday Night Football decided to try to make Deshaun Watson a redemption story. They did a whole puff piece on him before the game, talking about all the things that he had to overcome.
Nick Chubb coming back from a brutal leg injury deserves a piece like that. Brandon Graham coming back from a torn Achilles deserves that. Hell, Kyler Murray and Jared Goff deserve that.
A guy who was credibly accused of over 20 different (yet horrifyingly similar) accounts of sexual crimes maaaaaaaybe shouldn’t get that same grace, right?
So after that game ended, the sentiment coming from a big part of the internet was, ‘Hey. What the hell? That guy sucks as a person.’ The general response from the weirdos was, ‘Who cares? He’s a ball player. Three-game winning streak. Why can’t we focus on what he does on the field?’
Those are all things that people without conscience, morals, regret, or shame say. In other words: bots.
Last Sunday, Watson got sacked a whopping eight times. The ‘Let’s focus on the football’ accounts were awfully quiet about that … And it was probably because they exploded.
Who thought a Super Team would work?
The Rams built one hell of a roster over the offseason. That’s undeniable. On paper (numbers-wise), they were the best team in the NFL by a whooooole lot. We all know that the NFL not only makes it impossible for Super Teams to exist, but we also know that anything close to Super Teams ends up failing. Every. Single. Time.
That didn’t stop the Super Team talk from happening. No real human being would ignore the history of every super awesome roster that has been built … But a clanker sure would, and a clanker would absolutely latch onto a team that is prolifically awesome numbers-wise.
Then actually football gets played, the Rams are semi-bad, a bunch of bombs get dropped on a bunch of computers … and now we’re not hearing anything? Okay bud.
I’m supposed to believe that the online discourse around the Rams naturally went from ‘Sheesh, they’re world beaters' to ‘lol, fat kicker got fired’ and it doesn’t have anything to do with propaganda machines getting destroyed? Yeah right.

articles.title: China-EU auto trade consensus eases uncertainty, delivers mutual benefits - People's Daily Online
articles.summary: China-EU auto trade consensus eases uncertainty, delivers mutual benefits  People's Daily Online
articles.full_text:
Visitors try out a vehicle at the booth of Chinese automaker Li Auto during the 2026 Paris Motor Show in Paris, France, on Oct. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Huiwo)
BEIJING, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- The latest consensus reached between China and the European Union (EU) on hybrid vehicle trade is expected to reduce policy uncertainty, stabilize market expectations and safeguard the interests of businesses and consumers on both sides, paving the way for more predictable and mutually beneficial cooperation in the sector, analysts and industry representatives said.
Guided by the principles of mutual respect and equal consultation, the two sides, in the consensus reached during the latest meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism in Beijing, emphasized and confirmed three basic principles regarding hybrid vehicles: compliance with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules, non-discrimination and respect for facts.
Under the arrangement, China retains all its rights under the WTO framework, including the right to seek dispute settlement and trade compensation, while Chinese products will not be subject to discriminatory treatment. The arrangement also uses the trade volume recorded in 2025 as a baseline, allowing room for continued growth in Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to Europe.
The consensus comes against the backdrop of rapidly expanding Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the European market. In 2024, the EU imposed additional countervailing duties of up to 35.3 percent on Chinese-made battery electric vehicles, while hybrid vehicles were not subject to the additional tariffs.
Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to Europe subsequently surged. According to Eurostat, the EU imported 107,000 hybrid vehicles from China in 2024, with the figure rising to 302,000 in 2025.
Fu Xin, a senior partner at Jincheng Tongda & Neal Law Firm in Beijing, described the outcome as a breakthrough, noting that using the 2025 volume as the baseline accommodates the reasonable concerns of the Chinese automotive industry and its expectations for stable growth.
"Admittedly, quota restrictions will constrain excessively rapid growth by Chinese automakers, but they will encourage companies to compete on quality and pursue higher profit margins through higher-value-added products, in line with China's broader goal of promoting high-quality foreign trade development," noted Shi Xiaoli, director of the WTO Law Research Center at the China University of Political Science and Law.
For Chinese automakers, one of the most immediate benefits of the consensus is a substantial reduction in policy uncertainty surrounding exports to Europe.
Fu noted that growing uncertainty in trade and investment policies in recent years has made it increasingly difficult for Chinese automakers to formulate long-term business strategies.
The latest consensus, he said, will give Chinese companies operating in Europe a more stable framework of rules for the foreseeable future, allowing them to plan exports, investment and production with greater confidence.
Chinese automaker BYD said the consensus has effectively managed trade differences, prevented further escalation and taken into account the realities and legitimate concerns of industries on both sides, creating favorable conditions for sustainable cooperation.
At the 2026 Paris Motor Show, BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li disclosed the company's plans to expand its manufacturing presence in Europe. BYD's plant in Hungary is scheduled to begin large-scale production in the fourth quarter of this year. The company is also planning to establish its second and third manufacturing facilities in Europe, with France among the potential locations.
European automakers have extensive experience in automotive hardware, design and vehicle lifecycle management, while Chinese companies have competitive strengths in battery supply chains, intelligent driving and software technologies. These complementary advantages offer considerable scope for technological cooperation between the two sides, analysts noted.
Highlighting the strong complementarity between the two industries, Chinese carmaker Chery Group said closer cooperation would benefit businesses and consumers on both sides while contributing to the stability of global automotive supply chains.
Cooperation between Chinese and European companies could combine their respective strengths to improve vehicle quality, noted Andrea Levy, president of the Turin Motor Show.
Beyond the immediate benefits for trade, experts said that against the backdrop of rising trade protectionism and growing uncertainty across the global economy, the choice by the two major economies of dialogue over confrontation to resolve differences sends a positive signal in itself.
The China Association of Automobile Manufacturers said managing differences through institutionalized consultations and resolving disputes through cooperation rather than confrontation represented a rational choice that served the fundamental interests of both sides.
Responding to claims that the consensus was the result of EU pressure, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce stressed Friday that the understanding on hybrid vehicle trade is reciprocal and mutually beneficial, dismissing such claims as entirely unfounded.
The purpose of China-EU economic and trade consultations is to properly manage differences and address each other's concerns through dialogue and consultation, the spokesperson said, calling on both sides to demonstrate sincerity in resolving problems.

articles.title: The limits of China’s trade concessions to Europe - The Business Times
articles.summary: The limits of China’s trade concessions to Europe  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
Beijing’s agreement to curb hybrid car imports into Europe is a calculated compromise to preserve access
WHENEVER Beijing is confronted with complaints about its industrial overcapacity, its standard response is to reject them, insisting that Chinese manufacturers owe their success to innovation and competitiveness rather than unfair state support.
Just earlier in September, China’s Commerce Ministry was denouncing voluntary export restraints as a violation of World Trade Organization rules.
Yet on Oct 9, China reached an understanding with the European Union that could substantially restrict its exports of hybrid cars to the bloc. Rather than curbing its own exports, Beijing appears to have accepted limits imposed by Europe on imports.
Under the reported arrangement, imports from China would initially be limited to 350,000 hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles annually, with the quota increasing by 6 per cent each year from 2028 to 2030.
European officials say the restrictions could cut Chinese exports by more than half compared with projected 2026 volumes. Beijing, however, has presented the arrangement as allowing continued export growth from its 2025 baseline.
The deal addresses a tactical shift in the market. When the EU imposed tariffs on pure battery electric vehicles in 2024, Chinese carmakers rapidly expanded their shipments of hybrid and plug-in hybrid models to maintain momentum in Europe without incurring high duty penalties. Capping hybrids closes that crucial loophole.
The precise terms have yet to be finalised, but the concession raises a question: Why would Beijing accept limits on sales to one of its most important overseas markets, especially when Chinese carmakers face fierce competition and thin profit margins at home, and overseas demand has become increasingly important to China’s manufacturing sector?
A tactical concession
The answer lies in what China has not conceded.
Beijing has made no commitment to change the industrial policies that have helped turn it into a manufacturing powerhouse. Nor has it accepted Europe’s broader accusations of excess capacity.
Instead, China appears to have calculated that ceding ground on cars – an industry of enormous political importance to Europe – is preferable to risking a much wider confrontation over Chinese exports. The concession is costly, but carefully limited.
In Europe, the automotive industry is more than an economic sector; it is a major employer, a source of national industrial pride, and a politically powerful constituency.
Days before the Beijing talks, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz pushed for stronger European trade-defence measures, including more forceful restrictions on access to the EU’s single market.
Germany’s position was especially significant. Berlin has traditionally been more cautious than Paris about confronting China economically, not least because German automakers have substantial operations in China and remain vulnerable to retaliation.
The negotiations were already under way, so the Franco-German intervention cannot be credited with bringing Beijing to the table. But it raised the prospect that a dispute over hybrid cars could become part of a broader European response to Chinese manufacturing competition across multiple sectors.
The agreement also came ahead of a European Council meeting on Oct 15 and 16, when EU leaders were expected to consider whether tougher trade measures are needed to address their widening trade imbalance with China. That was a risk Beijing had good reason to avoid.
The US has effectively closed much of its automotive market to Chinese imports through prohibitive tariffs, leaving Europe as one of the few major wealthy markets where Chinese carmakers can expand.
China also has far more at stake in Europe than vehicles. The EU recorded a goods trade deficit with China of about 360 billion euros (US$403.8 billion) in 2025, illustrating the massive scale of European demand for Chinese manufactured products.
With domestic consumption struggling to absorb China’s enormous output, Beijing must keep that market open. It faced a choice: Allow hybrid exports to surge and risk provoking stronger European retaliation, or accept limits in one sector to safeguard broader market access.
Shifting from exports to local production
The automotive industry also offers Beijing and Chinese manufacturers ways to adapt. Restrictions on imported vehicles are bound to accelerate a transition already under way: moving from exporting built cars to manufacturing them directly inside Europe.
BYD is preparing to begin production in Hungary and considering additional manufacturing sites in France and Spain, while aiming to employ over 40,000 people in Europe by 2030. Leapmotor is pursuing European assembly through its partnership with Stellantis.
For Chinese manufacturers, this trade-off is considerable. Building factories in Europe requires heavy capital expenditure and sacrifices some of the low-cost manufacturing advantages enjoyed at home. But local production offers a durable foothold in a lucrative market, insulating Chinese brands from trade protectionism.
For European policymakers, the results will be mixed. Chinese-owned factories create local jobs and support regional supply chains, but established European carmakers will now have to compete with Chinese rivals operating on European soil, bypassing import duties – although EU regulators are already exploring ways to prevent these plants from becoming simple assembly hubs for Chinese components.
Europe may succeed in reducing imports of Chinese-made cars without actually reducing the market share of Chinese brands; influencing where the cars are assembled, but not whether European consumers buy them.
European governments could even find themselves competing against one another to attract investment from the very Chinese manufacturers whose exports they sought to restrain.
There is also an internal complication for Beijing. Overseas manufacturing may help its leading carmakers expand internationally, but smaller manufacturers may lack the resources to follow. What serves China’s broader diplomatic interests may not serve every Chinese company’s commercial interests.
Pragmatism, not retreat
The automotive dispute is only one component of a friction-filled economic relationship spanning chemicals, plastics and green technology. Beijing, already managing severe trade tensions with Washington, has no desire to open a full-scale trade war with Brussels.
Other elements of the recent deal mirror this pragmatic calculus. China agreed to facilitate export licensing for rare earths and permanent magnets, whose supply bottlenecks have threatened European manufacturing.
For European companies, more predictable access to these materials would be valuable. But China has not agreed to abolish its export controls or guarantee specific quantities. It retains authority over the licensing system and therefore much of the economic leverage that comes with it.
Nor is economic dependence strictly one-sided. A 2026 study by the European think-tank, Jacques Delors Institute, identified 41 critical product categories where China relies on the EU for over 80 per cent of its imports, including specialised industrial machinery and advanced pharmaceuticals. Europe remains vital to Chinese industry as both a buyer and a supplier.
China’s agreement on hybrid vehicles suggests an acknowledgement that its manufacturing dominance no longer guarantees unrestricted access to foreign markets.
But the concession may not buy Beijing the breathing space it hopes for. The EU is already considering further restrictions on Chinese competition in chemicals, machinery and other industries, while tightening access to public procurement and state support.
Beijing has shown that it is prepared to negotiate limits on exports in a politically sensitive sector. It has not accepted Europe’s broader diagnosis of industrial overcapacity, much less agreed to change the economic policies behind it.
And if Europe continues to demand concessions across other industries, China will face an increasingly difficult choice: How much of its export growth is it prepared to sacrifice to preserve access to foreign markets? THE STRAITS TIMES

articles.title: Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania - BBC
articles.summary: Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania  BBCAlbanian police fire rubber bullets as student protests rage  ReutersAlbanian PM blames ‘foreign hands’ for unrest as student protests intensify  Al JazeeraAlbania PM refuses to resign as student protesters attack government buildings  Financial TimesViolent Albanian protests sparked by luxury Trump resort ramp up amid demands for PM to resign  The Independent
articles.full_text:
Demonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row.
Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests.
The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time.
Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement, with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration.
Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street.
The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday.
During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard.
Here the crowds swelled to far larger numbers than on previous days.
Riot police faced a steady hail of cobble stones and fireworks, and responded with barrage after barrage of tear gas, some of the canisters landing far back in the crowds, causing panic.
Incensed by the gas, the crowds waited for it to clear, then renewed their attacks.
Black smoke from a burning vehicle and the sirens of police cars and ambulances split the afternoon.
As dusk fell, police special forces arrived to reinforce the riot police.
Many people have been injured on both sides, 80 people have been charged with disorder so far, and hundreds more have been arrested, or are under investigation.
The centre of the Tirana looks increasingly like a war zone, scattered with broken glass and burnt debris.
George, a 19-year-old medical student who works as an electrician to fund his studies, stood near the burnt-out education ministry building, a scarf wrapped round his face and goggles covering his eyes.
He is one of the thousands who have taken part in the increasingly intense protests which began in early June.
In his gloved hands he clutched two rocks intended for the police.
Asked if he was concerned about injuring them, he said: "We have mothers too. We have family too.
"We were peaceful for 135 days. Now we are trying to do like in France… we are trying to make a revolution.
"Our government doesn't want peace, so we are using violence."
Many of the protesters were even younger. Klea, 17, is in her first year of university in Tirana.
She said: "All the students are boycotting their university classes and left school to fight for our rights."
She alleged there were provocateurs among the protesters, smashing up stores and banks, to discredit the demonstrations.
Socialist Party Prime Minister Edi Rama has been in power for 13 years and has dominated Albanian politics, much like his main rival Sali Berisha, of the opposition Democratic Party, did for decades.
The students say they are against "the whole corrupt political class". So what is the alternative?
Osman Stafa, a prominent journalist for the News24 channel, who also describes himself as an activist for change, called for a "neutral, caretaker government for one year, to organise new elections".
The irony for the wider European community during this latest wave of unrest is that Rama has long been viewed favourably by the EU, which Albania aspires to join.
In a social media post on Saturday morning, he urged Albanian to "not forget that we have achieved extraordinary things".
He blamed the protests on the opposition Democratic Party, and on what he called "the sinister agenda of foreign actors, intent on halting our progress" towards EU membership, which he has promised by 2030.
He did not name which "foreign actors" he had in mind.
The latest protests have seriously tarnished Rama's carefully cultivated image as a charming leader, steering his country towards prosperity.
Parallel to the protests, a series of investigations by the special prosecution service also threaten his rule.
Set up under EU and US pressure in 2019, the prosecutors recently arrested the powerful secret service chief Vlora Hyseni.
She stands accused of helping a prominent businessman, former government official, and personal friend of Rama, Ergys Agasi, evade justice. The 39-year-old is under arrest.
Agasi, speaking through his lawyer, denied the allegations against him and said he had nothing to do with corruption. Hyseni told prosecutors that she contacted Agasi to try to recruit him to the intelligence services.
Several Albanian media outlets claim he acted as an intermediary between the prime minister and organised criminal groups.
Rama has admitted that he knows Agasi but denies any knowledge of illegal transactions.
"Edi Rama is caught between a rock and a hard place," Lutfi Dervishi, a political analyst and university lecturer, told the BBC.
"He's the victim of his own success. By concentrating so much power in his own hands, he has made himself the only person the people blame for their grievances."
Rama's Socialist Party has a comfortable majority, with 83 out of 140 seats in the Albanian Parliament. The next parliamentary elections are not due till 2029.

articles.title: Bank of England governor walks out of IMF summit in protest against Russia - The Guardian
articles.summary: Bank of England governor walks out of IMF summit in protest against Russia  The GuardianIMFC chair says global economy resilient; delegates walk out on Russian official  ReutersDelegates walked out of IMF steering committee meeting in Bangkok when Russian official spoke: Sources  The Straits TimesIMFC chair Al-Jadaan says all members supported chair's statement despite walkout  DevdiscourseUkraine's central bank chief welcomes walkout during Russian remark...
articles.full_text:
The Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, has taken part in a walkout of finance leaders who left an International Monetary Fund meeting in protest against Russian involvement.
Bailey joined counterparts from France, Germany and a number of Scandinavian and Baltic countries who left the session in Bangkok when the Russian finance minister, Anton Siluanov, addressed the group in Russian.
The Bank of England confirmed that Bailey took part.
The president of the German Bundesbank, Joachim Nagel, said nearly half of all delegates took part in the joint departure when Siluanov started speaking.
“The Ukraine war is existential for us in Europe,” one European diplomat told the Reuters news agency.
“We cannot normalise relations with Russia.”
The walkout was acknowledged by the chair of the IMF’s steering committee, the Saudi finance minister, Mohammed al-Jadaan.
Al-Jadaan said: “We came here for a reason, and we achieved it. Look at this chair statement, it clearly says that all members agreed to the statement, so that’s what matters.”
Germany had warned against efforts to bring Russia back on to the international stage. Siluanov attended a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bankers this year.
The US has been supportive, with the treasury undersecretary Erin Browne telling Reuters that Washington supported Russia’s presence despite concerns from European countries.
The meeting in the Thai capital heard that the global economy was showing remarkable resilience despite Russia’s war against Ukraine, and in spite of the issues around the strait of Hormuz caused by the US’s and Israel’s bombing campaign.
However, al-Jadaan added that there was no room for complacency, amid public debt levels and high bond market rates.
A statement from al-Jadaan after the IMF meeting said: “The global economy has weathered the latest in a series of shocks better than expected, but buffers have been eroded, and resilience cannot be taken for granted.”
He added: “Escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security.”

articles.title: ECB's Lagarde says bond selloff will slow inflation - CNBC
articles.summary: ECB's Lagarde says bond selloff will slow inflation  CNBC
articles.full_text:
A selloff in bonds is making borrowing more expensive in the euro zone, curbing economic growth and ultimately inflation, European Central Bank president Christine Lagarde said on Saturday.
Bond yields around the world have surged in recent weeks, with debt-laden France among the hardest hit, on the back of worries about debt and inflation as well as growing competition for credit from AI investments.
Lagarde said this would make it harder than the ECB had projected last month for consumers to absorb higher fuel prices from the Iran war.
"While growth has been resilient, financing conditions have tightened, with long-term interest rates rising notably since our last meeting," Lagarde told fellow central bankers and finance ministers gathering in Bangkok. "This will slow growth and reduce pass-through by more than projected in our September exercise."
The ECB has raised interest rates twice in the last four months and a further hike is expected in December, which would take its policy rate to 2.75% — a level it considers restrictive, or curtailing economic activity.
Fellow ECB policymaker Joachim Nagel hinted at more policy tightening ahead, although he added that the central bank would decide at each meeting based on incoming data.
"We are fighting against inflation, I'm of the opinion that the job is not done so far," the Bundesbank president told a DZ Bank event in the Thai capital. "I do see that maybe we have to do more."
Speaking alongside Nagel, his Finnish colleague Olli Rehn said the ECB would watch out for "second-round effects" from energy inflation on other prices and wages.
"There is no sign of second-round effects, but we will stay vigilant because they might creep in quietly like a cat in socks," Rehn said.

articles.title: Despite global headwinds and the ongoing energy shock, the euro area economy has so far proved resilient. - Christine Lagarde: IMFC Statement - Zprávy Kurzy.cz
articles.summary: Despite global headwinds and the ongoing energy shock, the euro area economy has so far proved resilient. - Christine Lagarde: IMFC Statement  Zprávy Kurzy.cz
articles.full_text:
Despite global headwinds and the ongoing energy shock, the euro area economy has so far proved resilient. - Christine Lagarde: IMFC Statement
- SPEECH
IMFC Statement
Statement by Christine Lagarde, President of the ECB, at the fifty-fourth meeting of the International Monetary and Financial Committee
IMF Annual Meetings, 17 October 2026
Introduction
The global economy has proven surprisingly resilient in the face of high uncertainty. The conflict in the Middle East continues to expose energy markets to sharp swings. Trade tensions and protectionist measures are weighing on confidence and contributing to a reconfiguration of trade flows. The global economy has held up thanks in part to the rise of artificial intelligence, with investment in technology supporting activity and trade, particularly in economies integrated into technology value chains. Risks nonetheless remain tilted to the downside for growth and to the upside for inflation. A return to an international economic order grounded in openness, predictability and the rule of law would help trade and investment flourish.
Economic activity
Despite global headwinds and the ongoing energy shock, the euro area economy has so far proved resilient. Growth was broad-based across most euro area countries and sectors in the first half of 2026. The September ECB staff projections foresee growth of 0.9% in 2026, 1.4% in 2027 and 1.5% in 2028.
As the energy shock fades over the medium term, the projections see domestic demand benefitting from a recovery in real income over the medium term, driven by lower energy inflation and a resilient labour market. Rising government spending on infrastructure and defence, complemented by investment in AI and digital technologies, should also support growth. Export growth should pick up on the back of strengthening foreign demand, also driven by AI.
The medium-term outlook is surrounded by uncertainty over how intense and long-lasting the Middle East conflict will be, and how the resulting shocks might propagate through the economy. Risks to growth are assessed to be on the downside.
Fiscal sustainability remains a crucial anchor for broader economic stability. It is important to maintain sound fiscal policies, including by adhering to fiscal rules, and, where debt is high, to consolidate, re-prioritise spending and enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of public finances to rebuild buffers. Governments should strive to ensure that any fiscal response to the energy shock is temporary, targeted and tailored.
In addition, policies that strengthen resilience to climate change can improve the economy’s ability to absorb climate-related shocks. These efforts should be complemented by structural policies that promote labour market participation, equip the workforce with the skills needed in an AI-driven economy and facilitate the diffusion of new technologies. Priorities include advancing the savings and investments union, improving access to risk capital and creating better conditions for innovative firms to scale up across the Single Market.
Inflation
Headline inflation increased to 3.8% in September, mostly reflecting a surge in energy inflation, and, to a lesser extent, an increase in food and services inflation. Core inflation increased slightly to 2.5%. The range of underlying inflation measures remained broadly stable in September and wages have so far shown no material response to the energy shock.
Looking ahead, higher energy prices are expected to keep headline inflation well above target into the first half of 2027 and to gradually feed through to core and food inflation. Headline inflation is expected to decline after the first quarter as energy inflation falls, returning to around target towards the end of 2027. The risks to the inflation outlook are to the upside due, in particular, to the Middle East conflict and Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine. A more intense or persistent energy shock could strengthen indirect and second-round effects, resulting in higher and more persistent inflation. Extreme weather could push up food prices. By contrast, a sustainable resolution of geopolitical conflicts, weaker energy pass-through or more risk-averse financial markets could lower inflation.
Monetary policy
The Governing Council decided to raise the key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points in September, following an increase of the same size in June.
Our interest rate decisions are based on our reaction function, which comprises three criteria: our assessment of the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data, the dynamics of underlying inflation; and the strength of monetary policy transmission.
The inflation outlook points to higher inflation ahead, especially in the short term, given the latest developments in energy markets. However, we see no evidence at this stage of significant pass-through of energy prices to other prices and wages, beyond what we have already included in our projections. And while growth has been resilient, financing conditions have tightened, with long-term interest rates rising notably since our last meeting. This will slow growth and reduce pass-through by more than projected in our September exercise.
Taking these three criteria together, the energy shock is too large to “look through” but a measured response remains appropriate to keep inflation in check.
In setting future policy, we will make a comprehensive assessment of the incoming data based on our reaction function. In July, the Governing Council decided on the operational features and the onboarding process for the enhanced EUREP, the Eurosystem repo facility for central banks that was announced earlier this year. The new facility supports the smooth transmission of monetary policy and reinforces the international role of the euro. More than 30 central banks have expressed interest in EUREP in the past six months.
Financial stability
Sources of risk and vulnerabilities for euro area financial stability remain high. Continued geopolitical tensions, fiscal challenges and uncertainties around accelerated AI adoption continue to be causes for concern. The widespread concentration of critical third-party service providers introduces single points of failure for both financial and non-financial institutions. New frontier AI models have increased cyber risks and operational vulnerabilities.
Euro area banks maintain strong capital and liquidity buffers and robust profitability, together with healthy and stable asset quality. These solid fundamentals should help navigate ongoing geopolitical uncertainties and effectively support lending to the economy. Strengthened prudential regulation and supervision since the global financial crisis has helped leave euro area banks in a strong position to withstand the unfolding economic challenges.
Shocks could expose vulnerabilities among non-bank financial intermediaries, notably from concentrated AI-related exposures, amplifying market stress and creating spillovers across financial sectors. Banks’ exposures to non-banks and vulnerable firms could expose funding and credit vulnerabilities.
Stress in private credit markets has continued, with private credit funds reporting outflows and reactivating redemption gates. Private market “semi-liquid funds” that allow for redemptions are becoming more prevalent, which could lead to greater liquidity mismatches in the future, but euro area financial institutions have limited direct exposure to private credit. This means, for now, that private credit in isolation is unlikely to be a source of financial instability in the euro area.
Payment systems
Central bank money must evolve to fulfil the needs of an increasingly digital economy. The Eurosystem is at the forefront of this evolution, bringing the stability and trust of central bank money to digital retail payments and tokenised finance in Europe. In the retail space we are preparing to complement cash with its digital equivalent – the digital euro – for day-to-day payments. The digital euro will further stimulate innovation and competition in retail payments, ensuring that the continued co-existence of public and private solutions underpins Europe’s strategic autonomy in payments. To lay the groundwork for a seamless and secure launch, we will run a 12-month internal pilot in the second half of 2027. Adopting the Regulation on the establishment of the digital euro by the end of 2026 is key to making this possible.
In the wholesale space, the Eurosystem is developing new capabilities to ensure that central bank money can settle transactions in the growing market of tokenised assets. Pontes – the Eurosystem’s distributed ledger technology (DLT) solution that went live on 21 September – marks the first step in implementing our strategy to enable the development of a European tokenised ecosystem. This vision will be advanced under the Appia initiative, which aims to deliver a blueprint for this ecosystem based on common standards, shared network infrastructure and European governance.
International cooperation
We value the work of our global institutions and fora, particularly those that promote global macroeconomic and financial stability. We welcome the recent completion of the three major IMF reviews (Comprehensive Surveillance Review, Financial Sector Assessment Program Review and Review of Program Design and Conditionality), which strengthen the role of the IMF at the centre of the global financial safety net. Climate-related work should remain fully anchored in IMF operations, particularly surveillance. Multilateral efforts to help tackle global imbalances support coordination of domestic action that is required to minimise the risks from disorderly adjustment. The IMF’s analytical work on global imbalances and its improvements to the methodology for assessing external balances provide a strong basis for these efforts.
