articles.summary: Seventy years ago, Britain led the way on nuclear power. Then we stopped  The TelegraphLabour urged to slash 'outdated' red tape to 'reclaim Britain's place as a global nuclear leader'  GB NewsUK nuclear power lifecycle: design and risk takeaways for civil engineers  Geomechanics.ioBuild It Better: Why Nuclear Regulatory Reform Is Key to Britain’s Energy Future  Sizewell CNuclear power becomes UK political consensus but can it deliver?  Montel Ne...
articles.full_text:
In 1956, Calder Hall in Cumbria became the world’s first commercial-scale nuclear power station. Some of the world’s best scientists, and engineers came together to help build and deliver an industry that would become the envy of the world – right here in the UK. Then, gradually, we stopped.
Seventy years on, the UK is embarking on another major infrastructure programme with nuclear power at its heart. The question is, however, what would the country look like today had we kept building?
You only have to look across the Channel. March 6, 1974 is a date that arguably changed French energy history forever. That day, the country’s prime minister, Pierre Messmer, announced a programme to build nuclear power stations across France. And they built at scale. Today, approximately 70 per cent of France’s electricity comes from nuclear energy. In the UK, nuclear generates only around 12 per cent.
Seventy years ago, Britain led the way on nuclear power. Then we stopped
Now is the time to build on what we started with infrastructure that will provide cheaper and more secure electricity to future generations

articles.title: Cost of living protests hit Belgium, Italy, Portugal and France - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Cost of living protests hit Belgium, Italy, Portugal and France  Al JazeeraViolent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze in France as over 1,000 arrested after protests  BBCProtests across France spiral into riots and looting  Financial Times‘If we burn, you burn’: hundreds arrested at protests across France – in pictures  The GuardianHistoric clock tower falls as France burns on day of violent protests  The Telegraph
articles.full_text:
Hundreds of thousands of Europeans have taken to the streets in separate, uncoordinated demonstrations to protest against the rising cost of living in their countries.
Saturday’s wave of unrest in Belgium, France, Italy and Portugal has put pressure on governments across the European Union.
France experienced one of its most turbulent days of protests in decades, with more than 550,000 people joining demonstrations, according to the Ministry of Interior, and police facing off with protesters across the country.
The marches, which followed weeks of student protests, degenerated into clashes, looting and fires after violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said 1,200 people were arrested and 150 police officers were hurt. “It’s a miracle the toll wasn’t higher,” he said as he visited officers deployed in central Paris.
Dozens of shops were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux, Limoges, Lille, Toulouse and Strasbourg, the French news agency AFP reported.
Whole streets in the capital “have been devastated”, Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said.
A fire set by masked protesters in Limoges largely destroyed the more than 140-year-old town hall, while city halls in Marseille and Lille were broken into and vandalised. In Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office.
President Emmanuel Macron said on X that those responsible would be “prosecuted and punished”.
In Belgium’s capital, Brussels – which has already seen weeks of protests by students against university registration fees – police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters, whom they accused of launching missiles at them and setting fires.
In Liege, a smaller city east of Brussels, police also deployed water cannon to break up demonstrations. Police did not say how many people attended.
Meanwhile, in the Portuguese capital of Lisbon, an estimated tens of thousands of protesters marched against the cost of living crisis, low wages and an inability to access housing in major cities. House prices in Portugal have more than doubled since 2017, while rents for new leases have increased nearly as much.
Portuguese Parliamentary Affairs Minister Carlos Abreu Amorim said on Friday that the “government will not yield to shouts from the street”. Protesters said their leaders are “out of touch” with the problem.
Italy
In Milan, rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire in the city centre, emptying Piazza del Duomo and a luxury arcade that would usually be full of shoppers.
A march against wars and rising living costs began peacefully, but masked protesters threw stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and set fire to barricades made from bar tables.
Police used water cannon and tear gas to disperse the crowds.
At least two police officers were injured, and about 50 demonstrators, many of them minors, were detained, the Italian LaPresse news agency reported.
Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned the violence.
“Demonstrating is a right. Setting our cities ablaze is not,” she wrote on X, blaming “hooligans who exploit demonstrations to sow chaos”.
Milan’s centre-left mayor, Giuseppe Sala, said “the reasons for the protests were understandable. The violence against law enforcement and serious damage to the city are not justifiable.”
In Bologna, police also reported that, alongside peaceful rallies, protesters threw stones and clashed with officers.
French protests spill over
Although protests in the other countries did not reach the same scale as the rallies in France, they may be a sign of discontent spilling over, Alberto Alemanno, professor of EU law and policy at HEC Paris Business School, told Al Jazeera.
“France is the epicentre of this movement … and there are signs now that this is spreading beyond France,” Alemanno said.
He said Saturday’s protests may not be the last in many of these countries and new hotspots could emerge.
In Greece, Germany, and Austria, the “early stages” of a movement are emerging, with mobilisation expected “in the coming week”, he said.
They are not a single movement, he explained, but several protests happening at the same time, with some “shared grievances”: underfunded education, rising living costs and, for students, uncertain prospects after graduation.
The unrest comes at a crucial time for Europe, Alemanno said, as the continent prepares for an “unprecedented super-cycle of national elections” in the coming 12 months, with votes scheduled in Spain, France, Italy and Poland.
“Inevitably, all these protests, all these mobilisations, are going to be at the centre of the political conversation,” Alemanno said.

articles.title: Will Paramount’s creation of Skydance test France’s cultural exception? - Modern Ghana
articles.summary: Will Paramount’s creation of Skydance test France’s cultural exception?  Modern Ghana
articles.full_text:
The completion this month of Paramount's $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery has created Skydance: a media behemoth that, as a result of the transaction, comprises some of Hollywood's most recognisable studios, including Warner Brothers, Paramount Pictures, HBO, Paramount +, a vast television portfolio, as well as news platforms, CNN and CBS.
The takeover was months in the making and garnered much public attention. What started as a tête-à-tête bidding war at the end of 2025 against Netflix culminated in a federal ruling against the 12 US states that tried to block the transaction on antitrust grounds at the end of September – just a week before final approval.
Read more Paramount completes takeover of Warner Bros, creating media behemoth Skydance
As film industry opponents feared job cuts, media groups worried about the editorial independence of a news platform under David Ellison, whose family has close ties to Republican US President Donald Trump. But from a French perspective, the development may cultivate a narrative that is less a question of whether yet another media giant can succeed in presenting true competition against the likes of Netflix or Canal+, and more about how a heavily indebted, consolidated global studio can operate profitably inside of one of the world's most protected audiovisual markets.
Creative works and cultural products are required to be handled differently when it comes to international trade laws, according to France's “cultural exception” policy. It hinges on a unique arrangement: international films and platforms may sell to French audiences, but they must actively contribute to preserve, invest in and stimulate France's creative economy. Ellison's deal therefore interrogates whether this principle can remain viable when the counterparty becomes larger, more leveraged and more focused on global scale.
Can Skydance afford French content?
Skydance began life with nearly $80 billion in debt, though it aims to reduce company costs by $6 billion in “structural and tech-stack cost savings” over the next three years, according tothe Financial Times. One of its first post-merger moves has included price increases on Discovery+, while reports indicate the firm's plans to combine the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services into a single platform or bundle.
This doesn't make French investment impossible. Indeed, consolidation may benefit French cinema by increasing the amount the company is required to invest locally under France's SMAD regime.
Introduced in 2021 and enforced by France's multimedia regulator, Arcom, the SMAD regime requires any foreign on-demand audiovisual service provider targeting France to contribute 20-25 percent of its French revenue towards European and French-language productions. A subsequent Paramount-HBO operation would aggregate subscription revenue, increasing the firm's local content obligations.
Read more Paramount CEO says politics fueling Warner Bros. merger battle
In the streaming universe, a related battle is underway among Netflix, Prime Video and Disney+. In July, the platforms filed appeals with France's highest administrative court – the Conseil d' État – to contest an amendment to the rule introduced in January this year that requires them to dedicate 20 percent of their investment requirement in French content specifically to animation, documentaries and live performance programming. The streamers argue that this “over-regulation” infringes on creative freedom and creates an unsustainable financial burden. But the court has not yet issued a final ruling on the legal challenges.
"These new rules suddenly double our obligation to invest in these genres, target streaming services exclusively and end up dictating our content offerings without taking audience expectations into account," Pauline Dauvin, vice president of Netflix France, said in an opinion column.
Pledging plurality
But scale does not guarantee cultural diversity.
Considering that the deal would enable Skydance to wield significant purchase power alongside other Hollywood heavyweights Sony, Disney and Universal, the transaction was submitted to the European Commission (EC) for regional approval, which it passed in July, subject to specific conditions.
At film production level, the EC found the conglomerate's studios to be suitably competitive. But at a distribution level, it stipulated that the company would need to unravel its ties from its Universal-Paramount joint venture, United International Pictures, within thirteen months of financial close, noting a “high concentration” in European Economic Area markets.
The transaction would have meant Skydance had advantageous distribution channels leading to “worse rental and distribution terms for cinema operators, ultimately disadvantaging consumers”, the EC wrote. It added that the conglomerate would also need to refrain from entering joint distribution arrangements for ten years and to avoid sharing releases with those also handling Universal or Disney rights in relevant markets.
Such redress is important for French exhibitors and distributors. While it does not prevent Skydance from fulfilling its role as a formidable supplier of content – indeed, as part of the firm's legally binding antitrust settlements with the 12 US states and the US Department of Justice, Skydance is required to produce at least 30 films per year for its first two years; rising to 32 films for the subsequent three, with penalties for shortfalls – it at least preserves a measure of plurality in how its films reach French cinemas.
Bloody broadcast
The key question perhaps is what type of content receives the funds?
In a joint statement titled “Bleeding public broadcasting: the shame of the Republic” and published last month via the Civil Society of Authors, Directors and Producers, France's leading film production and director unions, including the Trade Union for independent film, animation and audiovisual production (SPI), expressed fear that a merged giant is likely to favour global franchises, English-language formats and algorithm-friendly brands over smaller French films and original dramas.
Watch more Cannes, Canal+, Bolloré, blacklists: Is France's cultural diversity under threat?
In the context of bargaining asymmetry, it is possible that independent French producers – already navigating funding pressures and platform concentration – could come face-to-face with a single transatlantic buyer with the capacity to demand self-serving favourable rights and production models. And with every euro of compliance likely to be contested, there is potential for the long-term value of French intellectual property to erode, even where headline investment obligations are formally met.
'Chronologie des médias' under strain?
France's chronologie des médias constitutes a pillar of its system. It is a framework that sees box office features wait around 15-17 months before moving from screen to subscription platforms. The delay serves to protect cinema owners and ticket sales while channelling levies into the state-managed National Centre for Cinema and Moving Image's financial ecosystem.
And so Skydance's creation sharpens this tension. If the group wants its blockbusters to reach French viewers quickly, it must either respect the long release date windows or limit its cinema-wide releases (and box office turnover). But with a leveraged deal that puts the firm under pressure to monetise its strongest franchises across as many territories and platforms as possible – leaning on speed and scale, either option is likely to cost.
The danger is perhaps less that Skydance will bypass France, and more that the country may concede to the pressures of international dominance, resulting in fewer, safer, more commercial films. The firm could balance French release windows and funding local content if it treats the market as strategic ground rather than a regulatory obstacle course. But debt service, revenue targets and shareholder pressure risk rendering French-language content as compliance costs over creative priority. A possible outcome is selective investment: visible flagship French productions alongside reduced appetite for mid-budget and independent work.

articles.title: Israeli settlers attack European diplomats in West Bank - The Guardian
articles.summary: Israeli settlers attack European diplomats in West Bank  The GuardianEuropean diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank  BBCIsraeli settlers attack European diplomats, beat French mayor  Le Monde.frIran war live: Israeli settlers attack EU diplomats; drones target Riyadh  Al JazeeraIsraeli settlers attack European diplomats and French mayor in West Bank, Belgium says  Sky News
articles.full_text:
Israeli settler militants have attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of Cambrai in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank, injuring three people and damaging a car, in the latest violent attempt to prevent Palestinians from harvesting olives on their own land.
Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground on Saturday.
The masked militant shouted “Vive la France” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife, and Vincent Dollmann, archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs.
The group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls.
Settlers first attacked a group working on the lower slopes of hills near Taybeh. As well as stealing olives, they kicked, abused and assaulted a Palestinian woman in her 70s and beat a man so badly he needed six stitches for a head injury.
Then they approached the diplomats and Badoux, who was in Taybeh for the launch of a twinning agreement with his town in northern France. During the attack, the militants smashed the window of an armoured car belonging to the Belgian mission.
Maxime Prévot, Belgium’s deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs, condemned the violence against Palestinians, foreign diplomats and journalists, and said his country would continue to push for European Union sanctions on settlers.
“Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack,” he said. “This violence cannot be separated from Israel’s illegal settlement policy … the occupation of the Palestinian territory must end.”
Palestinian residents of Taybeh have lived with years of escalating attacks from Israeli militants, but settlers had never targeted foreign diplomats there, said Father Bashar Fawadleh, the town’s parish priest.
“What happened today is not an isolated incident. It represents a deeply disturbing escalation in settler violence,” Fawadleh said.
Since the start of the annual olive harvest in late September, Israeli militants have used violence to stop Palestinians bringing in a crop that is economically and culturally vital to their communities.
Since 27 September, settlers have launched more than 170 attacks, Israeli rights group Yesh Din said. They killed at least four people, injured more than 100 and damaged thousands of trees, according to Palestinian authorities.
Even the presence of Israeli activists, diplomats, senior clergy and journalists no longer serves as a deterrence to extreme violence.
“If such violence can take place before international witnesses, one must ask what protection remains for local families and farmers when those witnesses are no longer present,” Fawadleh said. “No individual should have to risk physical assault simply to harvest olives from their own land.”
On Friday, Israeli militants attacked and severely injured Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine as she reported on the harvest in the town of Abu Falah. She required surgery on Saturday morning and is now in “moderate” condition, according to a spokesperson for Israel’s Beilinson hospital where she is being treated.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that America wants Israel to do more to deter attacks committed by settlers. “We’re very disturbed by those images and what we’re seeing,” Rubio said. “We’ve asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff.”
Israel had already severely restricted the harvest this year by imposing new rules barring Palestinians from trees located in Area C, an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.
Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, condemned the attacks and said police had opened an investigation. He said foreign diplomats risked attacks from Israeli civilians if they travelled in the occupied West Bank without military coordination.
Demanding diplomats give advance notification of travel violates both diplomatic conventions and international law, said one western diplomatic source who asked not to be named.
“Israel is in charge of security in Area B and C (the majority of the West Bank), so is obliged to assure safety there for all,” the source said.
A culture of near total impunity for Israeli violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has prompted former prime minister Ehud Olmert to call for the international criminal court to intervene.
Gadi Eisenkot, an opposition politician and former general hoping to unseat prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu in elections to be held later this month described the attack as “Jewish terror under the auspices of the Israeli government”.
Eisenkot backs Jewish Israeli expansion in occupied Palestine but wants militant violence brought under control because the attackers are “harming the settlement enterprise in [the West Bank] and national security”.

articles.title: Man, 22, dies after falling from top of the Arc de Triomphe - Metro.co.uk
articles.summary: Man, 22, dies after falling from top of the Arc de Triomphe  Metro.co.uk
articles.full_text:
A young man has died after falling from the top of the Arc de Triomphe.
The incident occurred at around 3pm in the 8th arrondissement at the top of the Champs-Élysées in Paris, France.
A 22-year-old male fell approximately 50 metres from the monument in front of several witnesses.
Emergency services, including firefighters, arrived quickly, but the man was pronounced dead at the scene, the prosecutor’s office announced.
Consequently, the landmark has been completely closed to the public.
Investigators are currently treating suicide as the leading hypothesis, believing that he ‘jumped’.
Sign up for all of the latest stories
While police explore the circumstances that led to the man’s death, it is not thought to be linked to protests in the French capital ‘at this stage’.
Law enforcement clashed with demonstrators in Paris and other cities today, firing tear gas and water cannons and making hundreds of arrests.
Some, wearing hoods and face coverings, launched fireworks and other objects at riot police, who were deployed around Place de la République.
Protesters broke windows at CNews and Europe 1 offices, and reports from the scene said they threw projectiles at the buildings.
Town hall buildings in Lille and Marseille were broken into, with a fire breaking out on the roof of Limoges City Hall.
Authorities also closed metro stations and dispersed gatherings near government buildings.
Insisting that people have the right to protest peacefully, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said there is no place for ‘arson, looting, and attacks’.
He described today as the most violent school protests in decades and criticised the ‘hard left’ who ‘openly called for revolt’.
Hundreds of thousands of people, mostly young people, took to the streets to demand better education and improved public school conditions.
This followed weeks of student-led protests against crumbling buildings, teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, and budget constraints.
Teachers, parents, nurses, human rights lawyers, and emergency service workers joined the students in solidarity.
This weekend’s unrest also stemmed from anger towards rising living costs, fuel prices, and the deteriorating social welfare system.
Shortly after midday, the Interior Ministry recorded around 140 protest actions outside the Paris region. Protests were initially reported to involve more than 32,000 people, but by evening, that figure rose to over half a million.
Backing the rallies, the CGT, one of France’s major labour unions, echoed demands for ‘higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services that meet people’s needs’.
The protests increased pressure on President Emmanuel Macron’s government ahead of next April’s presidential election.
Macron, who first took office in 2017, responded to the demonstrators by saying there is ‘no place for violence in our Republic’, stating that those who have ‘vandalised and attacked’ will be ‘prosecuted and punished’.

articles.title: Is The Far Right Inevitable In Europe? - Glasgow Guardian
articles.summary: Is The Far Right Inevitable In Europe?  Glasgow Guardian
articles.full_text:
How the recent electoral results of Germany and Sweden portray a rather equivocal future for extremist politics and human rights.
Far right support is surging in Europe. Far right, nationalist parties have always flitted in and out of European politics in both EU and state level. However, in recent years support for such parties has gained traction, with them gaining significant wins across several European elections.
Is the far right really becoming the new norm in Europe? Their popularity among ordinary Europeans seems to imply so.
Earlier this September, Germany voted for Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), at the regional election for Saxony-Anhalt. AfD, is a party with strict nationalist ideals about which groups of people can be considered “German” and cannot. Non-White populations coming from immigrant backgrounds seem to get the worst end of it.
AfD’s policies of segregating schools based on residence status, and towns based on immigrant status, may sound exorbitant. The problem is that such bold claims appear to be receiving support amongst the general population of Germans. Regional election results in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenberg-Western Pomerania show historic wins for AfD.
Germany has an infamous history related to the far right. Yet nearly a century later, echoes of Nazism are still prevalent in the political atmosphere. 43.8% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt and 38.2% of voters in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania appear to share the sentiment that the extreme right wing policies of the AfD would better their living conditions in the long run.
Both Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-West Pomerania have drastic unemployment rates that are well above the national average. The stagnant economic growth in Saxony-Anhalt and the low living wages of Mecklenburg-West Pomerania are causing these wealth disparities in the regions, placing a substantial number of their citizens in poverty.
These parties use asylum seekers and immigrants as the fundamental reason behind rising rates of disparity.
The narrative being that unemployment is due to immigrants hoarding the job markets. Lack of housing is due to the asylum seekers that enjoy free rent-less housing and increasing crime rates are because of individuals that refuse to adapt to “superior” Western culture.
But where does that leave the asylum seekers? What happens to these individuals that are simply exercising their fundamental right to seek asylum?
Vilifying individuals that seek asylum, a right of all humans, endangers the entire concept of rights. The irony is that the West, which prides itself as the pinnacle of human rights, is also facilitating extremist politicians that want to scrap basic human rights. Nigel Farage of Reform UK for example, goes a step further, one of his key policies being to repeal the Human Rights Act 1998.
It’s the same case in Sweden. The Scandinavian nation, the epitome of human rights protection with its rankings in the Human Rights Index, is on the verge of overhauling its current immigration and asylum system. Endangering human rights of every individual, the same human rights that the country’s international identity is synonymous with.
Sweden’s current immigration policy is already one of the strictest in Europe. But does rising far right sentiment within the country mean that its citizens want complete restriction of migration?
In the 2026 general elections, left-wing and left-leaning parties won the majority of seats in parliament. However, the small three seat majority along with the strong opposition of right-wing parties puts Andersson’s Social Democratic Party (SDP) in a position to consider its current immigration policies.
The Sweden Democrats (SD), a former Neo-Nazi movement, is currently the third largest party in the Riksdag. SD was consistently ahead of polls in the run up to the general elections. Yet a scandal involving certain members of the party allegedly having associations with Russian Intelligence, broke into the limelight just days before polls opened.
Anti-Russian sentiment is popular in Sweden. It is ostensibly positive that a left-wing majority is in hold of the Riksdag. But it poses the question of whether the Swedish population voted against the SD due to the allegations concerning its staffer and not because of a switch in political attitude.
Although, while SD was very persuasive on stricter immigration and stronger borders, they overlooked the more important issues that the ordinary voters care more about. The economy, healthcare and education were the headlining issues in the run up to the elections. Not immigration, not refugees.
Sweden’s asylum system is already restrictive, courtesy to the 2015 refugee crisis. Hence, your ordinary Swedish person cares more about healthcare concerns and the economy rather than reforming an already strict migration policy.
The permanence of the far right that seems so strong at present is still up to debate. While AfD is popular in the Eastern parts of Germany, Berlin saw Die Linke gaining the largest share of the vote in the state elections. Both Liberal Democrats and the Green Party gained increased support in the 2026 England Local Elections.
The pattern here is how traditional parties that have been in power for decades are slowly losing their relevance in the face of novel, radical parties.
The surge of far right popularity intermingles with the populace rejecting the status quo. When countries rarely witness change, both politically and structurally, it is normal for voters to favour parties that offer radical solutions to their problems.
Yet, the far right is evidently more successful at getting their points of mandate across. They cleverly scapegoat the obvious minorities in society, compared to the way most left-wing parties focus on the ‘invisible’ 1%. As the name suggests, that is less feasibly viewed as a problem than those that physically look different to the majority of these European countries.
But it still would be wrong to portray the far right as the inevitable future of Europe. It’s constantly challenged, by equally strong opposition against it.
The rise of the far right is evident, yet as one can infer, a considerable rate of support is divided between left leaning parties as well. There’s a substantive distribution of left- and right-wing ideals that collectively oppose the traditional party systems of Europe.
This is a general era of major political upheaval and it’s necessary to recognize the fallibility of any party, regardless of their historic successes. While there is support, there will always be opposition from either side.

articles.title: The areas at risk of missile attacks as UK is ‘nowhere near ready’ for Iron Dome - The i Paper
articles.summary: The areas at risk of missile attacks as UK is ‘nowhere near ready’ for Iron Dome  The i PaperHow the Tories’ £10bn ‘Britannia Shield’ would protect UK from attacks  The TimesShield or sword: Does Britain need a more defensive military posture?  Britain’s WorldUK missile defences on a budget  The Australian Naval InstituteForeign Policy at the Conservative Party Conference  British Foreign Policy Group
articles.full_text:
Key RAF bases, the Royal Navy’s nuclear submarine hub and power stations would be most at risk from enemy missile strikes, said ex-military chiefs, who warned Kemi Badenoch’s £10bn British Iron Dome plan is insufficient to properly defend the country.
As concerns grow that Russia could attack a Nato country, head of the army, General Sir Roly Walker warned soldiers on Friday they could soon need to fight a war given the “extreme jeopardy in the world at the moment”.
This comes as at least 1,500 British, French and German troops are heading to Poland next month to rehears deploying to Ukraine if a ceasefire is agreed with Vladimir Putin’s forces.
Shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge said, unlike Israel’s Iron Dome, which focuses on short-range threats, the Tories’ Britannia Shield would counter longer-range drones and missiles, with new mobile radar systems bought. The largest sum of the £10bn would be spent on interceptor missile systems.
While military officials have not warned of an immediate attack, Waddington, Brize Norton, Benson, Odiham, Coningsby, Marham and Lossiemouth are the RAF’s seven main operating bases that enemies, such as Russia, would be likely to target in early salvos, experts warned.
RAF Fylingdales, which provides ballistic missile early warning and space surveillance for the UK and US, could also be a focus of the Russians, whose intercontinental ballistic missiles can reach the UK in 20 minutes.
Other key military targets would likely include the nuclear submarine base at Faslane on the Clyde, home to Britain’s Trident fleet, along with naval ports such as Portsmouth.
Critical civilian infrastructure like the UK’s three Liquefied Natural Gas hubs at the Isle of Grain in Kent and South Hook and Dragon would also be in the line of fire, but the risk of radioactive fallout meant nuclear power stations were not an obvious target, analysts said.
Shortage of Patriot interceptors
Britannia Shield envisages a three-pronged system with drones or missiles detected by new long-range radar before upgraded, unified command-and-control systems process data across the armed forces to analyse threats.
Then, interceptor missiles or counter-drone capabilities would be deployed to take out the threat. Cartlidge said it would protect critical national infrastructure and military bases.
But military experts, including General Sir Richard Barrons, said the Tories’ plan for an Israel-style Britannia Shield would do little to defend large cities in the UK.
They also highlighted a global shortage of expensive Patriot interceptors to defend against ballistic missile attacks.
Barrons, one of the three authors of the Strategic Defence Review, said the UK’s current air defence capability is “inadequate” and up to £120bn was needed to fund a proper defensive shield.
“The £10bn is a good start, but it won’t deliver the sort of protection that UK infrastructure and major metropolitan areas are going to need,” he told The i Paper.
“If you wanted to be sure enough that where most British people live had some protection from aircraft, missiles, and drones….there’s nowhere near enough money being put on the table to do that.”
What is the UK’s air defence capability?
The UK’s only current air defence capability that can intercept ballistic missiles are, six Type 45 Destroyers armed with Sea Viper systems that uses Aster surface-to-air missiles.
RAF Typhoons are able to shoot down enemy drones with Advanced Precision Kill Weapon Systems as well as short-range cruise missiles.
On the ground, Sky Sabre, the army’s air defence system, uses radar to detect threats up to 75 miles away, and can take out fighter jets, attack helicopters, drones, cruise missiles, and laser-guided smart bombs, while Rapid Sentry is the RAF’s short-range, counter-drone defence system.
Barrons said £10bn would bring better connectivity between the UK and Nato’s radar sensors and aircraft and fund more investment in new technology such as DragonFire, the laser system to be deployed on naval destroyers which can fry suicide drones.
But the UK currently has no Patriot battery systems, which cost up to £820m, to neutralise ballistic missiles, with a global shortage as Donald Trump’s war in the Gulf depleted stockpiles of the US-made interceptors.
Greg Bagwell, a former RAF air marshal, said: “A Patriot battery will cover maybe a city. It won’t really cover a small town or a base.
“So then you multiply that by the number of places you’ve got to protect, and you suddenly realise the problem.”
The UK should look to alternatives that could be made more quickly under license in the UK such as the Hanwha system in South Korea, Barrons said.
And it should use the £10bn to invest in homegrown interceptors like Cambridge Aerospace’s Skyhammer that can neutralise Shahed drones or cruise missiles, he added.
“I would argue you must protect those things that sustain the core of daily life, and so that’s enough power, enough water, enough food, and enough government,” said Barrons.
How could Russia attack the UK?
Dr Sidharth Kaushal, a senior research fellow for missiles and sea power at the Royal United Services Institute, said Russia would have to launch a strike on the UK from a bomber or a submarine launching cruise missiles.
“They don’t yet have enough Oreshnik intermediate range ballistic missiles to strike the UK credibly – they might do by the mid 2030s,” he said.
The hypersonic Oreshniks have been used by Russia to strike Ukraine and have a range of around 1,500 miles, so could in theory, reach London.
Dr Kaushal added: “A lot of the things they could fire over the east have to fly through a lot of [Nato] Allied airspace. So there’s limited chances of their getting here.”
Suppressing major air bases and destroying Astute-class nuclear submarines that can carry Tomahawk cruise missiles would be priorities in any Russian attack, he said.
But the Iskander ballistic missiles Vladimir Putin is using to hit Kyiv are not of a range that can strike the UK, he added.
Bagwell said Iran could not currently reach the UK with its long-range systems, but airbases and other military sites still faced the threat of drone attacks “parked in a truck 10 miles down the road”.
Do we have the soldiers needed for an Iron Dome?
The sort of integrated missile system envisaged by a British Iron Dome would not require more armed forces personnel to man it, which would be too expensive, said Barrons, with soldiers trained but only standing to during a crisis
“Most days you would hope very much you don’t need it. This would be set up, established, and run by industry,” Barrons said.
“Where you needed military people you would need a regular cadre go to work every day, but most of the manning would be done by reserves.
Such a system would be an extension of the armed forces digital kill web architecture using radar, satellite and acoustics, to make decisions about what weapons to shoot at.
The digital targeting web £1bn military integration initiative was introduced under the SDR to link military sensors in space, air, sea and land and cut battlefield decision-making times.
Bagwell said: “That will join these sensors up in a way that improves the UK’s ability to see what’s coming. But you still then have to do something about it.”
He pointed to RAF Fylingdales’ sophisticated radar that can detect ballistic missiles in space up to 3,000 miles away, but questioned if more focus should be placed on deterrent rather than warning of an attack.

The European Central Bank is expected to raise interest rates by 50 basis points by H1 2027, according to an ICICI Bank report. The move is attributed to high energy prices and persistent services inflation pushing price pressures above target.
The European Central Bank (ECB) is expected to raise interest rates by a cumulative 50 basis points by the first half of 2027 as elevated energy prices and persistent services inflation keep price pressures above target, according to a research report by ICICI Bank Global Markets.
The report said the ECB could deliver another 25 basis points rate hike before the end of 2026, followed by a further 25 basis points of tightening in the first half of 2027, assuming energy and commodity prices remain elevated.
Eurozone Inflation Accelerates
Eurozone headline inflation, measured by the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), accelerated to 3.8 per cent year-on-year in September from 3.2 per cent in August, driven largely by a sharp increase in energy prices.
Energy inflation rose to 18.9 per cent in September from 14.3 per cent in the previous month, while prices increased 4 per cent month-on-month, marking their fastest pace of growth in six months. The report attributed the surge to geopolitical disruptions in West Asia, warning that oil and gas prices could remain elevated for longer amid continuing tensions.
Underlying Price Pressures Persist
Underlying price pressures also persisted, with core inflation rising marginally to 2.5 per cent in September from 2.4 per cent in August. Services inflation increased to 3.2 per cent from 3 per cent, indicating continued domestic price pressures that could slow the return of inflation to the ECB's 2 per cent target.
However, core goods inflation remained unchanged at 1.2 per cent, suggesting that the pass-through of higher energy costs into core goods prices had remained relatively contained so far. The report said this trend offered some relief but warned that indirect effects from rising energy and transportation costs warranted monitoring.
Key Inflation Contributors
Transport prices emerged as a major contributor to headline inflation, rising 9.8 per cent year-on-year in September compared with 7.8 per cent in August. Prices in the housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels category also accelerated to 5.3 per cent from 4.3 per cent.
Food inflation edged up to 1.1 per cent in September from 0.8 per cent in August, partly reflecting a sharp increase in vegetable prices.
Implications for ECB Monetary Policy
ICICI Bank said the combination of elevated energy costs and sticky services inflation could complicate the ECB's efforts to bring inflation back to target, strengthening the case for further monetary tightening. (ANI)

Bangkok (Thailand) (AFP) – The artificial intelligence boom has been a key driver of global growth, but also poses economic risks should investment in the technology falter, experts and policymakers said this week at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.
Issued on:
Propelled by spending on data centres and microchips, AI has helped cushion the economic shock of rising global energy prices caused by war in the Middle East, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said in a report on Tuesday.
The fund's chief economist Silvana Tenreyro noted this week that global trade rose 8.3 percent between 2023 and 2025 -- a figure she said would be closer to 4.6 percent without AI-related products.
"It is everywhere in the global economy," Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said of AI on Friday.
"You see it in GDP. You see it in the stock market. You see it in the bond market... So it is here, and it's just the beginning."
But some top officials gathered in Bangkok this week cautioned against relying too heavily on AI investment.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh called AI the "most consequential change" to the global economy in his lifetime, and said it had "a huge benefit". Still, he warned the road ahead would be "bumpy".
"The path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one, bumpy in our understanding of the technology, bumpy because we really don't know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies," he said.
IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva similarly noted the AI boom's boost to global growth, but she told AFP that any slowdown in the industry "would be felt across the world".
"If there is loss of confidence and money runs away from AI, that can lead to financial stability risks," Georgieva said.
An IMF report released this week projected that a decline in AI investment could reduce global GDP by 0.4 percent by 2028.
"Weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction," the report said.
War and regulation
While AI investment and trade have softened the global economic impact of the Middle East war, economists at Moody's Analytics have warned that if the conflict drags on it could "puncture" the boom.
They said higher energy prices and tighter financial conditions could push up operating costs and interest rates, adding to doubts over "the long-term profitability and viability of AI business models".
"A drawn-out conflict would put serious strain on the economics behind AI investment," the group said.
The uncertainty around regulation has also clouded the technology's outlook.
Leaders like US President Donald Trump have urged more limited government regulation, even as some in the industry have called for legislation to mitigate risks.
Georgieva, the IMF chief, appeared on Friday to link such regulation to future investment.
"If there are no safeguards, then the risks may exceed the opportunities," she said in Bangkok.

articles.title: Europe’s Deep Heat: What It Takes to Make Enhanced Geothermal Systems Competitive - Bioengineer.org
articles.summary: Europe’s Deep Heat: What It Takes to Make Enhanced Geothermal Systems Competitive  Bioengineer.org
articles.full_text:
Deep beneath the European continent lies a vast reservoir of energy that never stops flowing. Unlike solar panels that sleep at night or wind turbines that stall in calm weather, geothermal heat from Earth’s interior can deliver electricity and warmth around the clock, whatever the sky is doing. A new study published in Nature Communications by Lukas Franken of the University of Edinburgh and Technische Universität Berlin, together with Elisabeth Zeyen and Tom Brown of TU Berlin, Orestis Angelidis of the University of Glasgow, and Daniel Friedrich of Edinburgh, has now mapped out in unprecedented detail how this resource could be woven into a carbon-neutral European energy system — and the answer turns out to hinge on a single number: the cost of drilling.
The technology in question is the enhanced geothermal system, or EGS. Conventional geothermal power plants tap naturally occurring reservoirs of hot water and steam, which limits them to geologically privileged regions such as Iceland or parts of Italy. EGS takes a different approach: engineers drill deep boreholes into hot but dry rock, inject water under pressure to create an artificial network of fractures, and then circulate fluid through that network to harvest heat. Because hot rock exists essentially everywhere at sufficient depth, EGS promises firm, dispatchable, low-emission energy with a footprint far smaller than wind or solar farms. The catch has always been economics — drilling kilometers into crystalline basement rock is expensive, and the learning curve that has slashed the price of solar modules and batteries has yet to materialize for deep wells.
To find out where and when EGS might actually pay off, the research team built a model of the entire European energy system spanning electricity, heating, and other sectors, and ran it through a series of scenarios for a net-zero future. The model co-optimizes investment and operation across technologies, meaning it does not simply ask whether EGS is technically feasible but whether a cost-minimizing, climate-compliant energy system would choose to build it at all, and where. Geological potential for EGS was mapped spatially across the continent, alongside the potential for wind, solar, and other renewables, so the model could weigh geothermal against its competitors region by region.
The headline finding is sobering but encouraging. If EGS plants remain at their current cost levels, a carbon-neutral Europe would still deploy roughly 20 to 30 gigawatts of thermal capacity from heat-generating or combined heat-and-power geothermal plants. That deployment is driven overwhelmingly by one customer: district heating networks. Cities across northern and eastern Europe rely on centralized heat distribution, and geothermal heat — which can be extracted at moderate depths without the extreme drilling costs of power generation — slots naturally into that market. In other words, the first wave of EGS expansion in Europe will likely warm buildings rather than light them.
Electricity is a different story. When the researchers modeled what happens if drilling costs fall by approximately 60 percent relative to 2020 levels, the picture changed dramatically. At that threshold, geothermal plants become competitive in electricity markets, bidding alongside wind, solar, and nuclear to supply the grid. The appeal is obvious: as Europe’s power system approaches 100 percent renewables, the value of firm capacity — generation that can be counted on during wind droughts and dark, still winter weeks — rises sharply. EGS offers exactly that, with capacity factors and flexibility that no battery fleet can match at scale.
But the spatial analysis reveals a structural constraint that no cost reduction can fully erase. The regions with the highest geological potential for EGS — areas where drilling is cheapest and rock temperatures are favorable — largely overlap with regions that also have excellent potential for wind and solar power. Where the sun shines and the wind blows, cheap renewables crowd out geothermal electricity. The places where EGS would be most valuable as a grid resource — regions with poor wind and solar resources — are precisely where its geological potential is weakest. This confined overlap of high geological potential with low renewable potential means the electricity market opportunity for EGS, while real, is geographically narrower than enthusiasts might hope.
Herein lies the central dilemma the study identifies. The bulk of Europe’s EGS market potential — the district heating segment — is spatially dispersed, scattered across hundreds of cities and towns rather than concentrated in a few geological sweet spots. Dispersed deployment means small projects, limited economies of scale, and slow learning. Yet the study shows that meaningful cost reductions of around 60 percent depend on exactly that: cumulative deployment and pan-European technology learning. The majority of the market therefore depends on cost reductions that only widespread adoption can deliver, while widespread adoption depends on those same cost reductions. It is a chicken-and-egg problem, and the authors’ conclusion is unambiguous: coordination is crucial. Without deliberate, pan-European stakeholder efforts — shared drilling campaigns, standardized well designs, coordinated learning across national industries — the learning curve may never steepen enough to unlock the electricity market.
The implications reach well beyond geology. For policymakers, the study suggests that support schemes for EGS should be designed around heat markets first, where the technology is already competitive at current costs, using district heating deployment as the training ground that drives drilling costs down. For investors, the 60 percent cost threshold provides a concrete benchmark: until drilling economics approach that level, geothermal electricity will remain a niche player in most of Europe, however attractive its firm-power profile. And for the broader energy transition, the work adds a crucial piece to the puzzle of clean firm power — the elusive category of always-available, zero-carbon generation that models increasingly show is essential once renewables dominate.
There are caveats, as with any scenario study. The analysis is based on cost and performance assumptions that carry uncertainty, and the authors note that their findings emphasize the importance of coordination precisely because the outcome is sensitive to how learning unfolds. The team also acknowledges collaboration with Project InnerSpace on North American EGS potential, though that work began after the analysis presented here was completed. Funding came from the UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council through the INTEGRATE and DISPATCH projects, and the underlying model builds on open energy system modeling tools developed in the group of Tom Brown at TU Berlin, whose PyPSA framework has become a standard for continental-scale energy system analysis.
What makes the study resonate beyond the technical community is the clarity of its message. Europe does not need to wait for a geothermal miracle to start harvesting its deep heat — district heating can carry the technology forward today, at current costs, to the tune of tens of gigawatts. But if Europe wants geothermal to become a pillar of its electricity supply, providing firm clean power in the places wind and solar cannot reach, it must treat drilling cost reduction as a collective industrial project, not a collection of isolated ventures. The heat is there. The question the study poses is whether Europe’s fragmented energy markets can organize themselves to drill toward it.

A super tanker has caught fire after striking a sea mine in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Saturday.
In a statement shared via Iranian state media, the IRGC's navy said a tanker carrying more than two million barrels of oil struck a mine whilst "attempting to pass through an unauthorised route" in the Strait, causing a "massive explosion" and a "fierce fire." It is unclear exactly where the incident took place.
Iran's Fars news agency posted a video appearing to show the vessel ablaze.
The IRGC navy accused the tanker of having turned off its positioning and radar systems in an effort to evade detection.
"The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and the consequence of defying Iranian regulations in the Strait of Hormuz is burning in the fire of trust in the terrorist US army," the IRGC navy added in its statement.
The Strait of Hormuz is a crucial gas and oil transit chokepoint that has been at the heart of tensions between Washington and Tehran since the Iran war broke out in late February.
Iran effectively cut off the passage, which usually carries around 25% of the world’s seaborne oil trade, following US and Israeli strikes on the country, prompting the US to impose a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
The US military has repeatedly pushed back on claims that the IRGC has control of the Strait, saying commercial vessels have continued to transit the region "despite unwarranted IRGC aggression."
Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of US Central Command (CENTCOM), said in an update on Friday that US forces were working with regional allies and partners in the shipping industry to help protect vessels navigating the Strait.
"Let me be clear, the Strait of Hormuz is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran," he said. "It remains open for business."

ECB officials see December rate hike as uncertainty clouds 2027 outlook
Policymakers see December as the likeliest time for a rate increase, while rising bond yields, high energy costs, AI investment and uncertainty over US policy complicate the outlook for next year
European Central Bank officials are preparing to finish 2026 with a third interest-rate increase, the last before an increasingly complex backdrop overshadows decisions next year.
While policymakers speaking this week in Bangkok kept open the option of acting in October, they pointed to December as the more likely timing for a hike that’s also widely anticipated among traders and economists.
But the discussions also revealed growing unease over issues including rising bond yields, high energy costs and the blistering investment boom in artificial intelligence.
“The tradeoffs for monetary policy are going to get more tricky,” Governing Council member Martins Kazaks said in an interview. “So far, the decisions have been relatively easy. But there’s a lot of uncertainty and very low visibility.”
The gathering in the Thai capital was dominated by warnings that the economy’s surprising resilience to the Middle East conflict will come under increasing strain. The euro zone, where investors have pushed up France’s borrowing costs due to its gaping budget deficit and political gridlock, was a focal point.
US midterm elections and an unpredictable response from President Donald Trump are adding to the uncertainty.
Policymakers signaled a preference for sticking with a quarterly pace of rate increases, suggesting continuity after being the first major central bank to hike rates since the war broke out. That would mean waiting until the Dec. 17 gathering, when they’ll have new economic forecasts.
“From a policymaker’s perspective, you want to take decisions when you have the largest amount of data available, and the next such meeting is December,” Governing Council member Gediminas Simkus said in a separate interview. “But you also can’t ignore the fact that we have a meeting in October.”
On the bright side, the Lithuanian and his colleagues pointed out that inflation heading toward 4 per cent — double the ECB’s target — hasn’t yet spread widely. At the same time, there are no signs that energy-driven price pressures are letting up.
On Friday, Brent oil hit $110 a barrel for the first time since May after Iran-backed Houthi rebels pummeled Saudi Arabia with missile and drone strikes, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged tit-for-tat attacks on energy infrastructure.
With wage negotiations looming next spring, the ECB is carefully analyzing how such shocks are “traveling through the economy,” President Christine Lagarde told CNN. “We are not seeing any of that yet, but we have to be extremely careful that little signs, indices of such secondary effects are visible.”
Officials are already pondering how restrictive monetary policy needs to become. The last two hikes, in June and September, took the deposit rate to the upper end of the range the ECB previously identified as neutral.
Additional moves — traders are betting on three by September next year — would start to damp economic activity just as a long-awaited recovery is taking hold.
“The market is pricing that we are going to have to do more,” Governing Council member Pierre Wunsch told Bloomberg TV. “It’s a base case that looks reasonable, but again, we are in a very uncertain world.”
Some of that uncertainty is originating in Europe, with French finances in the spotlight after a bond-market selloff stoked memories of the sovereign-debt crisis that shook the region through much of the 2010s.
Many participants in Bangkok, including IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva, argued that large budget deficits and debts must urgently be addressed, calling advanced economies the “worst offenders.”
While some ECB officials signaled optimism that the message investors sent to France has resonated with the government as it prepares key budget votes, others are already focused on how to respond if the situation deteriorates.
“The toolbox allows for quite a lot of instruments,” said Governing Council member Martin Kocher. “We are not at the stage where we need to discuss any of these instruments. But they are there if they are needed.”
The ECB’s work is overshadowed by increasing frustration among officials about Lagarde’s refusal to offer clarity on a possible early exit, according to people familiar with the matter.
The institution is in the midst of a major leadership overhaul, with Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel leaving in January, Chief Economist Philip Lane’s term expiring in May and Lagarde’s technically running through October 2027. Vice President Boris Vujcic joined in June.

articles.title: UK sees growing demand for help bridging gap between end of work and start of pension - The Guardian
articles.summary: UK sees growing demand for help bridging gap between end of work and start of pension  The GuardianFixed-term annuity interest rises as strong rates deliver State Pension-plus retirement income  IFA Magazine
articles.full_text:
Financial firms are reporting growing demand for a product that helps bridge the gap between stopping work and getting your pension.
Sales of retirement annuities have risen sharply during the last couple of years, and now advisers are seeing a fresh surge of interest in what they say is one of the market’s “lesser-known” options.
An annuity is a product that turns an individual’s pension pot into a regular, guaranteed income. The vast majority of people opt for one that provides an income for the rest of their life, called a lifetime annuity.
But more individuals are now buying a version that gives them an income for a set period – such as five or 10 years – and an agreed lump sum at the end. They can then decide what to do with that cash based on their circumstances at the time.
This type of product is called a fixed-term annuity, and the retirement specialist Standard Life says it can be a way to secure a guaranteed income for a set period while giving you the flexibility to review your options later.
After falling out of fashion, annuities have become more popular partly because of higher annuity rates and tax changes, but also because they offer some financial certainty during turbulent times.
On top of that, a fixed-term annuity can give some breathing space if, say, you don’t feel quite ready to sign up to a lifetime annuity or go into drawdown (where you withdraw a portion of your pension savings every year and leave the rest invested).
Standard Life says its data reveals there has been growing customer interest in fixed-term annuities this year, while its rival Canada Life said recently it had experienced a “significant rise in demand” for its version of this product.
So how much income might you get from a fixed-term annuity?
This week Standard Life said a 62-year-old with a £100,000 pension pot could currently get a guaranteed income of about £13,800 a year for five years, and would get a £50,000 lump sum at the end of the term.
This level of income is higher than the full new state pension of £12,548 a year. You get that when you reach state pension age, which has started to rise from 66 and will hit 67 in April 2028.
According to the latest Standard Life research, 62 is, on average, the age when people would like to retire. So someone could use a fixed-term annuity to fund the period between stopping work and getting their state pension, providing some financial certainty.
Nick Flynn at Canada Life says these types of products are resonating with retirees “because they solve real challenges, helping retirees buy time before committing to drawdown or purchasing a lifetime annuity”.
He adds: “Customers are choosing the product to bridge the gap to state pension or defined benefit pension start dates, help fund specific commitments such as mortgage payments or school fees, or stabilise income in the earlier years of retirement.”
Changes to the inheritance tax (IHT) treatment of pensions, announced by Rachel Reeves in the 2024 autumn budget, have helped give annuities a new lease of life.
The then chancellor announced that from April 2027, money left in a defined contribution (AKA money purchase) pension after someone’s death will no longer be exempt from IHT. All private pensions and most workplace schemes are defined contribution.
The changes mean “unused” pension savings could be taxed as part of someone’s estate if they exceed the IHT threshold. Unused funds are money in a pension pot that has not been used to claim an income, such as buying an annuity.
However, the insurer Legal & General says it surveyed 2,000 UK adults aged 50-plus earlier this year, and found misconceptions and confusion about annuities remained “widespread”.
For example, only 35% of respondents correctly identified a lifetime annuity as the retirement option that guaranteed an income for life. Meanwhile, 30% felt that annuities were too difficult to understand.
But L&G says: “Annuities are actually quite simple. They let you exchange some or all of your pension savings for a guaranteed income.”
However, it adds: “They are not right for everyone. Annuities generally cannot be changed once set up or cancelled after the cooling-off period.”
L&G has a myth-busting guide on its website.

articles.title: EU summit in Brussels: European powers intensify war drive against Russia - World Socialist Web Site
articles.summary: EU summit in Brussels: European powers intensify war drive against Russia  World Socialist Web Site
articles.full_text:
The EU summit held on Thursday and Friday in Brussels was an expression of the dangerous escalation of the international war crisis. While the Trump administration, amid its conflict with the European powers, is seeking at least for the moment a certain accommodation with Russia, the EU governments, led by Berlin, are pressing for the continuation and expansion of the Ukraine war. They want to shoulder an increasing share of the financial and military burdens themselves and build Europe into an independent military power.
This is accompanied by an escalation that threatens to provoke a direct war between NATO and Russia, including nuclear war. At the same time, the summit discussions on rearmament, “competitiveness,” trade war and migration underscore that the war drive abroad is inseparably linked to intensified social attacks and authoritarian measures at home.
Conflicts between Washington and Europe
At the center of the summit was the demonstrative support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Following an agreement with Putin on Russian diesel supplies, Trump had eased sanctions and criticized Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. He also demanded a change in Ukraine’s leadership. The European governments, by contrast, are determined to continue attacks on Russia’s energy infrastructure and tighten sanctions.
European Council President António Costa declared on Friday, standing alongside Zelensky: “Now is not the time to withdraw support for Ukraine. Now is not the time to ease sanctions against Russia.” Instead, the EU must increase its support and pressure on Russia. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced preparations for a 22nd package of sanctions.
The German government is taking a particularly aggressive stance. Chancellor Friedrich Merz declared that the EU must “once again ... increase” its funding for Kiev in order to “provide lasting support” to Ukraine. This was necessary, he said, to defend “the political order of Europe.” The conflict with Washington now also concerns control over approximately €210 billion in frozen Russian central bank assets in Europe. According to reports, US negotiators want to use part of these assets in negotiations with Moscow. Merz brusquely rejected this: “That is our affair, and we will decide on it.”
Behind these differences lie rival geostrategic and economic interests. The European powers fear that Trump could conclude an agreement with Putin that would undermine their own war aims and influence in Eastern Europe. At the same time, Ukraine’s war effort remains dependent on American military technology and intelligence support. Reports of restrictions on the satellite-based Starshield system demonstrate this dependence particularly starkly.
Ever more billions for war
Zelensky put Ukraine’s war costs for 2027 at €155 billion and demanded at least €70 billion in additional European support. With this money, Ukraine could produce two to three times as many drones and massively increase military pressure on Russia. The EU has already set in motion a €90 billion loan for 2026 and 2027. No decision was reached in Brussels on the new demands for billions; the Commission has been tasked with developing financing options.
The scale of the sums already mobilized is enormous. According to a study by the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, the German government puts its Ukraine support to date, including commitments, at around €100 billion. Approximately €41.7 billion is recorded as direct aid to Ukraine, while another €22 billion consists of future military commitments and possible expenditures. Together, this amounts to €63.7 billion, of which approximately €56.3 billion is military aid. In addition, €35.9 billion has been spent predominantly on Ukrainian refugees in Germany. Not all of the budgeted funds recorded have yet been disbursed.
The political thrust of the Kiel study is revealing. Under a headline emphasizing that “only” €41.7 billion actually went to Ukraine, it stresses that spending on refugees does “not support the Ukrainian government in its defense.” This juxtaposition alone makes the political orientation clear: While support for refugees and other social expenditures face growing pressure for cuts, ever larger sums are to be mobilized for the war effort. Added to this are hundreds of billions more that are to flow into military budgets in the coming years.
Concrete preparations for a NATO-Russia war
Parallel to the summit, the military confrontation is intensifying. NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Alexus Grynkewich presented his “Theory of Victory” in Warsaw: “Block, Blunt, Break.” A potential attack is first to be repelled, then the opposing armed forces smashed, and finally the command, supply and production structures supporting them disabled. Grynkewich describes the strategy as defensive, but in a major war the planned operations could extend deep into Russian territory. He praised Germany as the “engine of NATO.”
At the same time, NATO conducted the nuclear war exercise “Steadfast Noon” in Italy this week, involving 17 countries, including German Tornado fighter jets. NATO describes it as a routine exercise without live nuclear weapons. Yet it rehearsed procedures for nuclear operations at a time when the risks of escalation are rapidly increasing.
Russia is responding to NATO’s constant provocations with nuclear threats. In early October, Putin warned that Russia could use its entire arsenal in the event of a blockade of Kaliningrad. Now, State Duma Deputy Alexei Zhuravlyov has told Lenta.ru that, in the event of a NATO attack, Russian nuclear strikes could target NATO headquarters, as well as US nuclear weapons bases in Germany, Belgium, Italy and Turkey. Zhuravlyov’s threat is not an official government statement. His remarks nevertheless demonstrate how concretely sections of the Russian establishment are discussing nuclear war in Europe.
Russian military commentators warn that NATO’s strategy could serve as a cover for “preemptive” strikes. They draw parallels to Hitler’s war of annihilation against the Soviet Union, which Nazi propaganda likewise justified as “defense” against an allegedly planned Soviet attack.
Regardless of NATO’s specific timetable for war, the mutual threats already demonstrate that an escalation could rapidly spiral out of control. In the Black Sea, Romania and Bulgaria are demanding additional NATO measures against Russia following drone attacks on merchant ships.
Rearmament and social devastation
Europe’s response to the war and the crisis of its alliance with Washington is a gigantic rearmament program. “ReArm Europe” is intended to make possible up to €800 billion in additional defense spending by 2030, while the SAFE program provides €150 billion in loans. In Germany, defense spending is to rise to approximately €140 billion in 2027—and to well over €200 billion in 2029. The German government wants to build the Bundeswehr into Europe’s strongest conventional army.
These sums have immediate social consequences. While debt rules are relaxed for rearmament, European governments are organizing historic cuts to social benefits and public services. Under the slogan of “competitiveness,” the EU summit adopted measures for deregulation, accelerated approval procedures and further economic restructuring. Jobs are being eliminated on a massive scale, wages cut and working conditions worsened.
The EU also wants to create new trade policy instruments to take tougher action, particularly against China. Merz stated that the Commission had been given a mandate to this end. Von der Leyen announced additional import restrictions.
The migration debate at the summit also revealed its reactionary direction. Italy, Denmark and Poland attacked Spain’s planned legalization of the residence status of around 600,000 migrants. Discussions included tightening detention provisions in border procedures and suspending asylum applications in times of crisis. In the Middle East, against the backdrop of the US-Israeli war of aggression against Iran, the summit focused above all on securing trade and energy routes.
As the EU advances its global war offensive and reactionary domestic agenda, tensions among the European imperialist powers are growing. The dispute over the next EU budget for 2028 to 2034 exposed these rivalries. Net contributors, such as Sweden, are refusing the higher contributions being demanded, while the EU seeks to mobilize additional funds for strategic and military projects. No agreement has yet been reached.
The extreme escalation of war is also a response to growing social and political opposition in Europe. In France, Spain and other countries, mass protests and strikes are developing against social cuts, militarism and authoritarian measures. Confronted with the deep crisis of the established parties, the ruling classes are attempting to divert this opposition outward through war propaganda and nationalism and force the population to rally behind their war policies.
But this course will only further intensify social antagonisms. The gigantic military expenditures, the destruction of jobs and social benefits, and the increasing attacks on democratic rights will not extinguish the resistance of the working class and youth but further fuel it. At the same time, the escalating confrontation with Russia threatens to plunge all of Europe into a nuclear world war.
The decisive task is to arm the growing opposition with an independent socialist perspective. The working class must organize independently of the established parties and unite its struggles across all national borders against capitalism, militarism and war. The nationalist and militarist project of the European governments must be opposed with the struggle for the United Socialist States of Europe.

Not every country experienced growth. Russia recorded the largest absolute decline, with its resident migrant population falling by approximately 4.3 million. Serbia, Ukraine, and several other Eastern European countries also recorded decreases.
Why Has Europe Become a Migration Hub?
Economic opportunities, EU freedom of movement, family reunification, and humanitarian protection have all contributed to Europe's growing migrant population.
An aging workforce has also increased demand for foreign workers in healthcare, construction, and hospitality. These pressures help explain broader immigration trends across developed economies.
Conflicts have also reshaped migration patterns, particularly the Syrian refugee crisis and Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
What Does Rising Immigration Mean for Europe?
Immigration can ease labor shortages, expand the tax base, and help offset demographic decline. However, rapid population growth can also strain housing, schools, and public services, especially when infrastructure fails to keep pace.
Policies governing work permits, housing, language training, and recognition of foreign qualifications help determine how successfully newcomers integrate. These challenges are particularly relevant as some countries also experience heightened emigration among their native-born populations.
Ultimately, Europe's migration story is not simply about attracting more people, but about how effectively countries accommodate and integrate them.
