Key Takeaways:
- EU leaders must decide this autumn on rules for Chinese goods entering the single market, conditions for Chinese investment, and limits on Chinese suppliers in critical infrastructure, while facing a €1 billion daily trade deficit and the risk of Chinese retaliation via critical minerals.
- Drawing on the U.S. experience, the article argues that Europe can pursue targeted restrictions and stability simultaneously, using trade-defence tools, the Foreign Subsidies Regulation, and the International Procurement Instrument without allowing a narrow deal to freeze broader action.
- On investment, it calls for making more conditions mandatory under the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act so Chinese projects generate local value rather than “screwdriver” assembly; on infrastructure, it urges extending high-risk supplier rules beyond 5G through the Cybersecurity Act revision.
This autumn, Europeans must decide on new terms of engagement with China. They are facing a surging EU trade deficit of €1bn a day, industrial deterioration across the continent and Chinese threats of economic coercion.
Trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic travels to Beijing this week for the final stretch of trade talks, just as Paris and Berlin publish a joint paper demanding tougher trade action against China. At a European Council summit later this month, leaders will be asked whether they wish to negotiate an agreement with China covering these issues—or whether instead to follow the Franco-German push and move to enforce European interests unilaterally by introducing tougher restrictions on China’s access to the single market.
In weighing this question, Europe’s leaders must settle three decisions: first, what rules to set for Chinese goods to enter the EU; second, what they want Chinese investment to contribute to European industry; and, third, where they should limit the roles of Chinese suppliers in critical infrastructure. Looming over all three choices is the geoeconomic reality that Beijing can retaliate—most critically, by restricting exports of critical minerals products to Europe.
The US experience
Recent US dealings with China offers guidance for how (and how not) to make such choices under threat of retaliation. In 2025, Washington assumed that imposing major tariff hikes would harm the Chinese economy and leave Beijing scrambling to make economic and political concessions. Instead, China responded by expanding restrictions on essential rare earth supplies. This put Western factories and defence production under immediate pressure. It forced the White House to de-escalate its tariff hikes and seek accommodation for a more predictable trade relationship.
Now, Washington is pressing ahead with targeted efforts to limit options for where Chinese companies sell, invest and operate. This includes restricting companies’ access to the US market beyond tariffs, while also curbing investment from China and increasingly banning the use of Chinese technology domestically. Despite China’s potent escalation options, the US is pursuing both stability and decoupling at the same time.
The lesson for Europeans is that talks and bargaining with Beijing can help contain escalation while enforcing their own rules across trade, investment and critical infrastructure.
How the EU navigates its season of decisions will determine whether it can successfully defend its industrial and security interests in the face of China’s threats of retaliation.
Three decisions for the EU
What China sells
Europe’s first decision is whether to accept a narrow trade settlement with China in October. Such a settlement—for example, focused on automotive exports, which the two sides are currently discussing—may ease some tensions. It could see China voluntarily limit the number of electric and hybrid vehicles it sends to the EU each year. Or it could involve expanding so-called “price undertakings” in which individual Chinese producers agree to market entry terms, such as minimum import prices, total volume limits or local investment commitments. Volkswagen Anhui, one of the German company’s China-based joint ventures, already agreed to such terms earlier this year.
However, this approach risks failing to address wider industrial challenges posed by the Chinese system. Sectors other than the car industry are already under pressure from China’s industrial policies, including batteries, wind equipment, robotics, machine tools, chemicals and biotechnologies. But a narrow agreement would leave these areas untouched.
Any deal the EU strikes must therefore address these particular issues and support a level of stability between the EU and China—while also preserving the bloc’s ability to tackle other distortions from China independently.
What the EU should do
Therefore, making a deal on one product cannot become a promise to tolerate distortions impacting on others. In the electric vehicle value chain, Brussels must retain its ability to launch anti-subsidy (and safeguard) investigations in other segments of the chain, like batteries, or sectors outside the scope of a settlement. The European Commission must also make use of the anti-circumvention tools it already has to close gaps created by Chinese producers redirecting exports through different locations or product categories. Unlike the Trump administration’s broad tariffs, trade defence measures calibrated to identified distortions would preserve competition in the single market while removing China’s artificial advantages.
The same logic must apply inside the single market, and Europe must maintain its autonomy to enforce a level playing field. This means the EU should be free to systematically launch and conclude investigations under the Foreign Subsidy Regulation across sectors where Chinese state financing is plausibly distorting competition in the single market. The bloc can also make assertive use of the international procurement instrument across every sector where documented procurement discrimination against European firms exists in China.
Furthermore, the EU must press ahead with upgrading its economic security toolbox, and make sure its contents are not beholden to any deal agreed with China. This includes developing a diversification instrument that could push firms in critical sectors to have a diversified supplier base (this could, for example, work by the EU placing tariffs on overdependent imports). It also means strengthening the anti-coercion instrument to lower the bar for activation, and adding a solidarity fund to compensate companies hit by retaliation and coercion.
Where China produces
Europe’s second decision is about what it expects in return when Chinese companies invest in the single market. Chinese investments in Europe (including Britain) have recovered from a previous lull, reaching almost €17bn in 2025 (nearly a quarter of all Chinese FDI), with 45% of that investment in the automotive and EV sector.
The problem for Europe is that, despite this rising investment, China’s exports are increasing at an even faster pace—supported by continued industrial policy support, persistently weak domestic demand and a weak yuan. Where Chinese investors are active in Europe, the risk persists that they will merely relocate final assembly while their supplier networks and technology remain tightly guarded. Without adequate safeguards, Chinese firms may set up “screwdriver factories” in the EU, which assemble largely pre-manufactured components, while retaining high-value activities in China. Indeed, Beijing has not only instructed its carmakers to follow this path, but also explicitly expanded its control levers to decide which automotive components are allowed for export.
What the EU should do
Europe’s trade and investment policies therefore have to work together. To ensure Chinese investors actually shift production to the continent, Europeans need to change the business arithmetic that makes exporting from China more profitable, whether by imposing tariffs or agreeing a managed trade deal. Where import barriers encourage Chinese investment, the EU must then ensure projects will develop local suppliers and support technology learning or transfer.
The EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, which is under negotiation, attempts to partially address this issue. Importantly, it marks a shift away from treating foreign investment in batteries, electric vehicles, solar power and critical raw materials as an automatic benefit. Under the plans, investments above €100m would have to meet four out of six conditions intended to generate industrial value in Europe (including introducing ownership limits, a joint venture condition, intellectual property sharing, local sourcing and more). Yet, as currently drafted, the only mandatory condition for foreign investors is to commit to local employment. The proposed design would create an à la carte system in which investors could avoid the requirements that are most important for supporting Europe’s industrial transition and scale-up.
It now falls to member states and the European Parliament to make more investment conditions mandatory if China wishes to enter Europe’s strategic industrial base. They should also future-proof the Industrial Accelerator Act by explicitly allowing the legislation to cover other sectors at the core of industrial competition, such as industrial robotics, wind equipment and medical technology.
What China controls
Europe’s third decision concerns where it allows Chinese suppliers a role in critical infrastructure and systems—and where they are excluded. Member states have in recent years strengthened their foreign investment screening powers and adopted a common approach to high-risk 5G suppliers. Yet the security risks today extend beyond these tools and sectors. They reach deep into European ports, energy systems and connected infrastructure.

Fed Chair Warsh’s non-committal stance weakened the US Dollar, boosted foreign currencies, and left inflation and rate expectations in focus.
Fed Chair Warsh Adopts a Non-Committal Stance and Shifts Away From Forward Guidance
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh signaled a notable shift in communication strategy during his remarks in Bangkok, stating explicitly that he does not prejudge upcoming meetings and emphasizing that the Fed is actively moving away from previewing its policy decisions. By offering no explicit forward guidance on the future trajectory of interest rates, Warsh’s non-committal commentary immediately impacted market sentiment. Consequently, market pricing for a potential rate hike at the October 27–28 meeting plummeted from roughly 28% down to about 15% or 16%, though a December rate increase remained heavily priced in near 90%. This dovish-by-omission approach introduced immediate selling pressure on the greenback, driving the Dollar Index (DXY) down toward 101.65—its lowest level since October 1—as it headed toward its first weekly decline in five weeks.
Divergent Global Central Bank Expectations and Currency Responses
The shift in US monetary policy expectations rippled across global foreign exchange markets, amplifying divergences between major central banks. In the United Kingdom, resilient economic data and subdued signs of second-round inflation drove a Reuters survey to show that 54 of 63 economists expect the Bank of England (BoE) to implement a 25-basis-point rate hike in November. This hawkish outlook pushed the British Pound (GBP/USD) above 1.3350, registering gains of over 0.61%. Simultaneously, modest narrowing in front-end Eurozone-US yield spreads, catalyzed by Warsh’s remarks, provided upward momentum for the Euro (EUR/USD) and positioned the currency for a potential bullish weekly reversal. Broadly speaking, Warsh welcomed a synchronized global tightening cycle with no free riders, allowing key interest rate differentials—such as the gap between US rates and the European Central Bank’s 2.5% rate—to remain stable.
Persistent Inflation Risks, Geopolitical Pressures, and Cautious Safe-Haven Sentiment
Underpinning these currency and interest rate movements are stubborn macroeconomic and geopolitical headwinds. Hotter-than-expected US Consumer Price Index (CPI) readings and a stronger-than-forecast 0.7% expansion in September industrial production underscore that underlying price pressures remain sticky and above the Fed’s 2% target. These domestic inflation risks are further aggravated by elevated Middle East supply concerns, highlighted by deadlocked US-Iran negotiations and escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis. Meanwhile, concerns over debt-funded AI investments triggered a sharp flight to safety, pulling the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield below 5.10% and supporting safe-haven assets. Despite lower yields and a softer US dollar, gold (XAU/USD) struggled to secure a robust recovery, trading below $4,200 as market participants continuously weighed safe-haven demand against the lingering prospect of future Fed tightening.

Martin Lewis has criticised proposals from Ofgem that could make tariffs for switchers more expensive.
The energy watchdog launched a consultation on Monday over plans that could see energy firms forced to pay consumers’ old suppliers when they switch away, in a move designed to protect providers from financial losses amid soaring energy prices.
The move could come in as soon as November, as Ofgem has argued suppliers could be left out of pocket if wholesale energy rates fall sharply and people leave in large numbers.
But the MoneySavingExpert founder has said it will "dampen competition" and could push the prices onto switchers.
In a blog post, Mr Lewis said: “In a nutshell, it means if wholesale energy prices drop sharply, the cheap fixes and switcher deals offered will be a lot more expensive, in order to protect energy firms' profits.”
He described the plan to introduce a “market stabilisation charge” as a form of “switching penalty” while the supplier market remains stable.
Ofgem announced at the end of August that it would be raising the energy price cap by four per cent in October to reflect the soaring price of gas caused by conflict in the Middle East.
Neil Kenward, interim director general of markets, said the consultation came as the market was expected to grow more volatile this winter.
“We’re preparing for what is likely to be a difficult winter for many households,” he said. “While the energy market is stronger than it was during the energy crisis, volatility remains, and the market stabilisation charge helps to protect consumers from that volatility.”
He added: “In volatile market conditions, it’s important that suppliers can continue to secure the energy their customers need without taking unsustainable risks.
“By acting now, we can help maintain a stable and resilient energy market and protect consumers from the costs and disruption that can arise when markets become unstable.”
The measure was previously put in place in April 2022 through to March 2024 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which sent energy markets reeling.
Ofgem said reactivating it would not automatically create charges or push up customer bills, stressing payments between suppliers would only be made if wholesale prices fell sharply enough.
Mr Lewis said despite the rising price of liquid natural gas, there was no risk of suppliers going bust – and some had even appeared to make a profit.
“I doubt we are at the domino risk of suppliers going bust in the way they did in the early twenties,” he said. “A good few energy firms have made large profits since then, and protecting them over winter by effectively dampening competition because it's 'not their fault' feels raw.
“After all, we don't take their profits off them when they make them 'through no fault'. Until now, my hope had been that at some point the Middle East situation would de-escalate, wholesale rates would drop.
“While it would take months for that to feed into the price cap, other cheaper tariffs would be available to switch to. That would still happen, but the savings could be nowhere near as good as otherwise.”
A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: "We are working with the regulator to build a stable energy market which puts consumers first."
The Independent has contacted Ofgem for further comment.

The proposed investment would be deployed as opportunities arise, with the company pursuing port concessions and logistics projects, including the proposed Vadhavan port on the western coast. Narayan said the amount was not tied to a fixed investment timetable and would depend on the outcome of bids.
"We are prepared to invest between $3 billion and $5 billion (in India)," he told a select group of journalists.
DP World, which has built an integrated Indian network spanning ports, rail and inland logistics, is seeking to expand its footprint as the world's most populous country looks to strengthen domestic connectivity and become a larger manufacturing and export hub.
The company announced an additional $5 billion India investment commitment in October 2025, over and above $3 billion invested in the country over three decades.
India's infrastructure push has delivered substantial improvements, Narayan said, but port and rail development and the processes governing project execution need to move faster.
"One always hopes things could happen faster," he said, pointing to the long wait for the Vadhavan project and arguing that infrastructure development should keep pace with progress in roads, airports and power.
DP World is prepared to bid for new opportunities, expand its rail network and increase port capacity, Narayan said. The company currently operates six port concessions in India and plans to increase its railheads from eight to 12, according to him.
India's growing economic scale makes it attractive despite historically weaker returns on invested capital, Narayan said. Currency depreciation, driven in part by the country's energy import bill, has weighed on returns, while infrastructure upgrades, digitisation and the shift towards renewable energy could improve the outlook.
The proposed investment would also help strengthen DP World's wider supply-chain network, rather than simply expand its Indian business, he said.
The investment push comes as disruptions around key West Asian maritime chokepoints force shipping companies to reroute cargo, add capacity and absorb higher operating costs.
Narayan said DP World's flagship Jebel Ali port in Dubai, which normally handles about 15 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) annually, was facing a severe reduction in activity because of restricted access. He said the disruption was affecting cargo flows well beyond the Gulf, creating congestion at ports and logistics facilities across parts of Asia and Africa.
The impact extends beyond the port itself, he said, because Jebel Ali serves as a major transshipment hub linking Asian manufacturing centres with markets in the Middle East, Africa and Europe.
DP World had expected Jebel Ali's port operations to generate about $1.2 billion in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA), but Narayan said the disruption would materially reduce the group's earnings outlook. He estimated that global EBITDA could fall to about $5.8 billion from a level of roughly $6.2 billion to $6.4 billion, with growth elsewhere cushioning part of the lost contribution.
The company is exploring alternative routes through other Gulf ports and overland connections, including routes through Saudi Arabia, Narayan said. But building replacement capacity takes time, and he estimated that new port capacity could take two to three years to develop.
"Port capacity is not created overnight," he said, warning that the full consequences of the disruption may take time to emerge.
The crisis also underscores the growing cost of building redundancy into supply chains. Companies that once prioritised lean inventories, low costs and just-in-time deliveries are increasingly seeking alternative suppliers, routes and production centres to reduce their exposure to geopolitical shocks.
Narayan said global trade now required substantially more shipping capacity to move less cargo than before, as longer routes and operational inefficiencies absorbed available capacity. Higher interest rates, fuel expenses and other operating costs were adding to the burden.
"Who do you think pays for all this disruption? You - as a consumer," he said, arguing that the additional costs would ultimately be passed through to buyers of goods.
He expects shorter supply chains and a greater emphasis on regional production to reshape trade flows over time, potentially increasing the importance of north-south trade between Asia, Africa and other emerging markets.
For India, the opportunity lies in expanding manufacturing and exports while building the port, rail and inland logistics infrastructure needed to connect producers with global markets.
Narayan said India's exports and imports currently account for a relatively small share of its overall economy, leaving considerable room for growth. A substantial increase in trade would require a corresponding expansion in logistics capacity, he said.
However, he cautioned that resilience would come at a cost. Maintaining alternative routes, suppliers and inventory buffers would make supply chains more expensive and capital-intensive than the lean systems businesses had previously pursued.
"The world has to come to peace," Narayan said, arguing that physical infrastructure alone cannot eliminate the risks posed by conflict.

To assist agricultural exporters in meeting European commercial and statutory benchmarks, CSX defines five operational pillars governing sustainable fruit packaging compliance:
100% FSC Chain-of-Custody Certification and Sustainable Forestry Traceability: Verifiable chain-of-custody documentation confirms raw paper substrates originate from responsibly managed forests, supporting options with 70% post-consumer recycled fiber content.
Biodegradable Corrugated Substrates and European EPR Compliance: Fully recyclable and compostable corrugated board formulations align with European PPWR targets, reducing plastic waste fees and supporting packaging lightweighting goals.
Food-Grade Direct Contact Safety and Eco-Friendly Soy-Based Inks: Non-toxic, odorless, water-based adhesives and soy-based printing inks replace petroleum-derived mineral oils, satisfying international food contact migration limits.
All-Paper Folding Structures Replacing Single-Use Plastic Punnets: Engineered mono-material corrugated geometries and folding paper punnets replace expanded polystyrene and single-use thermoformed plastic trays.
BSCI and SEDEX Factory Social Audits with ISO Management Systems: Internationally recognized third-party ethical audits validate workplace standards, environmental responsibility, and quality control systems across manufacturing facilities.
100% FSC Chain-of-Custody Certification and Sustainable Forestry Traceability
Statutory market access under the EU Deforestation Regulation dictates rigorous traceability across wood and paper fiber supply chains. The regulation requires commercial operators placing regulated forestry products on the EU market to provide verifiable due diligence demonstrating that packaging materials do not originate from deforested land or contribute to forest degradation. Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) chain-of-custody certification establishes the documented chain of custody required to verify that wood fiber originates from responsibly managed forests.
CSX manufactures fruit packaging using 100% paperboard materials sourced exclusively from FSC-certified forestry operations. Every production run carries certified chain-of-custody documentation, providing batch-level traceability that verifies sustainable harvesting practices. For enterprises pursuing specific circular economy targets, CSX provides corrugated board configurations incorporating up to 70% post-consumer recycled fiber content. This balanced fiber architecture maintains the high edge crush resistance (ECT) and stacking strength required for agricultural transit while lowering virgin resource consumption in alignment with European circularity directives.
Biodegradable Corrugated Substrates and European EPR Compliance
European packaging policies under the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation enforce aggressive targets to minimize packaging waste and enhance circular recyclability. National Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) schemes across France, Germany, Spain, and the Netherlands impose financial levies on packaging materials based on their recyclability rating, penalizing non-recyclable composite materials and unsegregated plastic liners.
Mono-material corrugated packaging provides a direct pathway to minimizing EPR compliance costs. CSX produces agricultural containers using 100% biodegradable and compostable corrugated paperboard that integrates smoothly into standard European municipal paper recycling streams. Using pure cellulose fiber structures simplifies the sorting process associated with multi-material composites. In addition, high-precision structural design reduces overall packaging tare weight without compromising box compression test (BCT) strength, lowering transport carbon emissions and directly reducing weight-based EPR disposal contributions for importing partners.
Food-Grade Direct Contact Safety and Eco-Friendly Soy-Based Inks
Packaging materials in direct contact with fresh produce must adhere to rigorous European food safety frameworks, including Framework Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004 and Good Manufacturing Practice Regulation (EC) No 2023/2006. These regulations mandate that packaging surfaces must not transfer chemical constituents into food in quantities that could endanger human health, alter food composition, or deteriorate sensory characteristics.
CSX formulates agricultural packaging to satisfy food-grade contact hygiene criteria across all internal and external surfaces. Corrugated flute bonding utilizes non-toxic, odorless, cross-linked water-based starch adhesives, preventing chemical volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions inside closed container environments. Surface printing employs natural soy-based inks in place of traditional petroleum-based mineral oil inks. Soy-based formulations avoid aromatic hydrocarbons (MOAH and MOSH), preventing mineral oil migration into edible fruit skins while delivering high-resolution brand printing, regulatory hazard pictograms, and traceability barcodes that remain sharp throughout cold-chain transit.
All-Paper Folding Structures Replacing Single-Use Plastic Punnets
European retail grocery chains enforce strict timelines to remove single-use plastics from fresh produce aisles. Mandates across major European markets restrict the use of expanded polystyrene (EPS) trays, thermoformed polyvinyl chloride (PVC) punnets, and non-recyclable plastic clamshell containers for fresh fruits and vegetables under 1.5 kilograms. Complying with these retail merchandising standards requires engineering functional all-paper alternatives.
CSX designs specialized all-paper agricultural containers and retail-ready packaging that completely replace disposable plastic hardware. For delicate soft fruits, CSX manufactures food-grade berry paper punnets and ventilated strawberry boxes engineered from high-strength kraft paperboard. These containers incorporate precision-cut side ventilation slits and integrated self-locking tabs, providing fruit visibility and dynamic airflow without relying on plastic film windows or plastic clip closures. To phase out internal non-recyclable padding, CSX replaces conventional thermoformed blister and synthetic foam trays with 100% recyclable die-cut cardboard inserts, securely cushioning produce within calibrated individual compartments. The resulting mono-material structure allows European consumers to dispose of the entire packaging unit into domestic paper recycling bins, satisfying the zero-plastic mandates of major European supermarket chains.
BSCI and SEDEX Factory Social Audits with ISO Management Systems

articles.full_text:
The EUR/JPY cross trades on a flat note around 177.30 during the early European trading hours on Friday. Traders remain on high alert for currency intervention from Japanese authorities to prop up the Japanese Yen (JPY).
Furthermore, hawkish comments from a Bank of Japan (BoJ) policymaker could provide some support to the JPY and act as a headwind for the cross. BoJ policy board member Junko Koeda said that there is no need to be excessively cautious about rate hikes given that upside inflation risks remain substantial.
Koeda further stated that the Japanese central bank should adjust its policy rate in a timely manner while keeping in mind the estimated range of the neutral interest rate.
On the Euro front, Citi analysts believe French debt concerns could prompt the European Central Bank (ECB) to pause interest rate hikes after December, or earlier if financial stress spreads across the Eurozone. The ECB is likely to leave its deposit rate unchanged at 2.50% in October but raise it by 25 basis points (bps) in December as inflation runs nearly double its 2% target, according to a Reuters poll.
Analysts at MUFG note that September was “a month of turmoil in global bond markets,” reflected in “the selling of foreign bonds by Japanese investors.” In contrast, they highlight that “foreign investors did not show the same aversion to fixed income” and instead recorded “a notable JPY 3,091bn worth of purchases of Japanese bonds.” With September also marking another BoJ rate increase, MUFG suggests this inflow “could be indicative of improved confidence in JGBs after three consecutive months of selling through to August.”
The bank also points to Japan Investment Trust data as “telling,” with “foreign equity purchases totalling JPY 1,360bn in September.” MUFG stresses that “the buying has picked up,” noting that “the 3mth sum of foreign equity purchases totalled JPY 3,949bn, a new record over a 3mth period.” They emphasise that this Investment Trust flow “captures households buying of foreign securities via NISA accounts” and that “the expanded NISA limits adopted in January 2024 continues to have a notable impact.” MUFG calculates that “annualising this 3mth flow implies an outflow of close to JPY 16trn (USD 100bn) and is an increasing negative yen factor.”
Looking ahead, MUFG argues that “providing tax-free opportunities to hold JGBs could well have an impact on the flows to foreign equity markets that is so evident today and given the scale of foreign equity purchases currently would be viewed as a clear yen positive.” Such a move “would be one policy initiative that would help the government reach a target of 40% of household financial assets being invested in domestic securities.” At present, MUFG notes that “nearly half of all household savings are parked in cash deposits and large portions of pensions and investment trusts are invested in foreign securities,” underscoring the potential for policy tweaks to redirect savings back toward domestic markets.
In the daily chart, EUR/JPY keeps a bearish near-term bias as spot holds beneath the 20-day Bollinger simple moving average (SMA) and well below the 100-day moving average. Price action sits in the lower half of the Bollinger envelope, while the Relative Strength Index (14) around 39 suggests subdued upside momentum and favors continued downside pressure unless resistance levels above are reclaimed.
On the topside, initial resistance level emerges at the 20-day Bollinger SMA near 178.20, en route to the 180.00 psychological level. Sustained trading above this level could pave the way to the upper boundary of Bollinger band at 180.75, with a more significant barrier at the 100-day moving average around 182.90.
On the downside, the lower limit of Bollinger band at 175.65 offers the next notable support. A clear break below this floor would open the door toward the October 20 low, 2025 of 175.34, followed by the October 2, 2025 low of 172.27.

The Japanese Yen (JPY) is one of the world’s most traded currencies. Its value is broadly determined by the performance of the Japanese economy, but more specifically by the Bank of Japan’s policy, the differential between Japanese and US bond yields, or risk sentiment among traders, among other factors.
One of the Bank of Japan’s mandates is currency control, so its moves are key for the Yen. The BoJ has directly intervened in currency markets sometimes, generally to lower the value of the Yen, although it refrains from doing it often due to political concerns of its main trading partners. The BoJ ultra-loose monetary policy between 2013 and 2024 caused the Yen to depreciate against its main currency peers due to an increasing policy divergence between the Bank of Japan and other main central banks. More recently, the gradually unwinding of this ultra-loose policy has given some support to the Yen.
Over the last decade, the BoJ’s stance of sticking to ultra-loose monetary policy has led to a widening policy divergence with other central banks, particularly with the US Federal Reserve. This supported a widening of the differential between the 10-year US and Japanese bonds, which favored the US Dollar against the Japanese Yen. The BoJ decision in 2024 to gradually abandon the ultra-loose policy, coupled with interest-rate cuts in other major central banks, is narrowing this differential.
The Japanese Yen is often seen as a safe-haven investment. This means that in times of market stress, investors are more likely to put their money in the Japanese currency due to its supposed reliability and stability. Turbulent times are likely to strengthen the Yen’s value against other currencies seen as more risky to invest in.

articles.title: Europe’s Climate Rules Bend Under Industrial Pressure - Impakter
articles.summary: Europe’s Climate Rules Bend Under Industrial Pressure  Impakter
articles.full_text:
Paris and Berlin move to soften the 2035 car emissions target
A provisional deal would drop the requirement for carmakers to close the final gap, and could bring Britain inside the bloc’s local-content rules.
France and Germany are close to an agreement that would ease the EU’s carbon rules for cars, according to diplomats. The Commission proposed last year that emissions from new cars fall 90% against 2021 levels by 2035, with manufacturers expected to reach 100% through low-carbon steel and alternative fuels. Under the Franco-German plan, the 90% figure would stand on its own, with no compensating measures required. German carmakers have wanted much the same.
The plan also touches the local-content rules attached to public procurement, auctions and subsidy schemes. France has argued these should cover goods made inside the EU; Germany and others want partners in automotive supply chains included.
For cars, the two capitals propose that “Made in Europe” extend to the 27 member states plus European partners that were inside the single market on 1 January 2020, Britain among them. That would come with conditions: full reciprocity, and alignment with EU rules on third-country investment and trade defence, which could require London to mirror the bloc’s limits on Chinese hybrid and electric vehicles.
Nothing is settled. Other member states and Parliament still have to agree.
Grid bottlenecks leave Britain paying to switch wind farms off
Payments to shut down turbines in one place and fire up gas plants in another have hit levels last seen in 2022, and they land on household bills.
Great Britain’s grid operator spent £47.9 million on Wednesday managing a mismatch it cannot yet fix with cables. Wind farms and hydro plants with roughly 9 gigawatts of capacity, enough for more than 8 million homes, were paid to stop generating, according to the consultancy LCP Delta, while gas and biomass plants were switched on elsewhere and extra power was bought from Europe through subsea links. One half-hour period alone cost £1.6 million.
September’s total reached £505 million, a monthly record, and the bill for the coming year is put at £3.2 billion. Households pay it.
The cause is not scarcity. Shivam Malhotra of LCP Delta said supplies were not tight; what is missing is the infrastructure to move power to where it is wanted, which leaves Scottish wind farms switched off for want of cabling to the south.
Neso says supplies stayed secure and that faster delivery of new transmission lines by the network owners could halve these costs by 2030.
States line up against OpenAI over its effect on minors
Eight attorneys general want damages, product changes for young users, and a pause on models that can improve themselves.
Eight states have filed suit against OpenAI in their own courts, accusing the company of putting children at risk through the way its products behave. Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana each allege breaches of consumer protection law. No group of states has moved against an AI firm in concert before.
The core claim concerns the distance between how the product is marketed and how it works. The filings argue the chatbot was designed to agree readily with users and to imitate warmth, and that this turns hazardous for people who are vulnerable. Iowa’s attorney general, Brenna Bird, said the firm assures the public of safety while the product hands out unsafe medical guidance and presents itself as a companion.
Beyond compensation, the states ask the courts to bar the company from building models that can upgrade themselves, unless it demonstrates those systems match human values.
OpenAI points to age-specific safeguards it says competitors lack, among them parental controls and prompts to take breaks, and argues any rules should apply across the industry.
BHP takes its Chilean copper union to court over stoppages
The miner wants $8.6 million from workers at Spence, arguing two shutdowns fell outside the agreed bargaining window.
BHP has sued the union representing workers at its Spence copper mine in northern Chile, according to a court filing seen by Reuters. The company says two stoppages in June and July significantly disrupted operations and were unlawful because they took place outside a scheduled negotiating period.
At issue is a bonus. The filing says the union was pressing for a special payment of 5 million pesos, around $5,100, for each member, money that sits outside the agreements already in place.
The union would not comment. BHP confirmed that it had gone to court.
Spence is the company’s second-largest operation in Chile, where it also runs Escondida, the biggest copper mine in the world. Strikes are a familiar feature of the Chilean copper industry, the largest in the world by output, though they usually come during contract talks rather than between them.

articles.summary: Euro gains as US Dollar weakens following Fed Warsh’s comments at IMF chat  www.tmgm.com
articles.full_text:
EUR/USD remains stronger after posting modest gains the previous day, trading around 1.1230 during Asian hours on Friday. The currency pair inches higher as the US Dollar (USD) declines following recent comments from key financial leaders.
Speaking at a fireside chat with International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva in Bangkok, US Federal Reserve (Fed) Chairman Kevin Warsh reiterated the Fed’s commitment to price stability while refusing to prejudge upcoming policy meetings. Warsh highlighted that an investment surge is currently the most significant upside force in the global economy.
Meanwhile, US Treasury Undersecretary for International Affairs, Erin Browne, called on the IMF to take a more assertive approach to identifying global imbalances and urged a balanced outlook considering positive US-led economic shocks. She further cautioned that sharp, disorderly currency moves could trigger volatility across broader financial markets.
However, the Greenback gained support from stronger-than-expected inflation data released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Thursday. The US Producer Price Index (PPI) surged 6.3% year-over-year in September, its largest gain since 2022, easily topping the market consensus of 5.3% and following a revised 5.6% increase in August. On a monthly basis, the PPI rose 1.3%, significantly outpacing the 0.5% analyst estimate. Core PPI, which excludes food and energy, also came in hotter than expected, rising 0.7% month-over-month and 5.0% year-over-year.
Despite the elevated inflation figures, market expectations regarding Federal Reserve interest rate decisions remained largely unchanged. According to the CME FedWatch Tool, traders are pricing in a 72% probability that the central bank will keep rates steady. However, expectations for a rate increase in December have climbed to 92%.
On the European front, upside momentum for the EUR/USD pair remains constrained due to political uncertainty in Europe, particularly in France. European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde emphasized that France must address its national debt challenges through fiscal consolidation, dampening speculation that the ECB might intervene by purchasing French bonds to contain rising yields.
While Lagarde noted that energy-driven inflation has not yet spread to the broader euro-area economy, supporting a cautious policy stance, ECB policymaker Gediminas Šimkus asserted that a rate hike this month remains an option if necessary. Markets continue to price in another ECB rate increase in December.
The Euro is the currency for the 20 European Union countries that belong to the Eurozone. It is the second most heavily traded currency in the world behind the US Dollar. In 2022, it accounted for 31% of all foreign exchange transactions, with an average daily turnover of over $2.2 trillion a day. EUR/USD is the most heavily traded currency pair in the world, accounting for an estimated 30% off all transactions, followed by EUR/JPY (4%), EUR/GBP (3%) and EUR/AUD (2%).
The European Central Bank (ECB) in Frankfurt, Germany, is the reserve bank for the Eurozone. The ECB sets interest rates and manages monetary policy. The ECB’s primary mandate is to maintain price stability, which means either controlling inflation or stimulating growth. Its primary tool is the raising or lowering of interest rates. Relatively high interest rates – or the expectation of higher rates – will usually benefit the Euro and vice versa. The ECB Governing Council makes monetary policy decisions at meetings held eight times a year. Decisions are made by heads of the Eurozone national banks and six permanent members, including the President of the ECB, Christine Lagarde.
Eurozone inflation data, measured by the Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), is an important econometric for the Euro. If inflation rises more than expected, especially if above the ECB’s 2% target, it obliges the ECB to raise interest rates to bring it back under control. Relatively high interest rates compared to its counterparts will usually benefit the Euro, as it makes the region more attractive as a place for global investors to park their money.
Data releases gauge the health of the economy and can impact on the Euro. Indicators such as GDP, Manufacturing and Services PMIs, employment, and consumer sentiment surveys can all influence the direction of the single currency. A strong economy is good for the Euro. Not only does it attract more foreign investment but it may encourage the ECB to put up interest rates, which will directly strengthen the Euro. Otherwise, if economic data is weak, the Euro is likely to fall. Economic data for the four largest economies in the euro area (Germany, France, Italy and Spain) are especially significant, as they account for 75% of the Eurozone’s economy.
Another significant data release for the Euro is the Trade Balance. This indicator measures the difference between what a country earns from its exports and what it spends on imports over a given period. If a country produces highly sought after exports then its currency will gain in value purely from the extra demand created from foreign buyers seeking to purchase these goods. Therefore, a positive net Trade Balance strengthens a currency and vice versa for a negative balance.

articles.title: Egypt’s Sisi seeks authorisation for defence assistance to Saudi Arabia - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Egypt’s Sisi seeks authorisation for defence assistance to Saudi Arabia  Al JazeeraEgypt's Sisi seeks parliament's backing to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked  ReutersEgypt’s Sisi seeks parliament approval to authorize support for Saudi Arabia  Arab NewsEgypt said to mull supporting defense of Saudi Arabia in face of Houthi attacks  The Times of IsraelEgyptian and Iranian Foreign Ministers Discuss De-escalation  Global Arab Network
articles.full_text:
Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has called for an emergency parliamentary session to authorise him to approve any requests from Saudi Arabia for defence assistance, if Riyadh were to ask.
Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy on Saturday, el-Sisi emphasised Cairo’s readiness to back the kingdom.
Egypt will “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia “in accordance with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and the directives of the Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman”, he said.
“I know that this matter requires the approval of the Egyptian parliament, and I hope that parliament will convene in an emergency session to give us this authorisation, if it is requested of us,” he said.
“I am not speaking in order for us to fight anyone or attack anyone. I am speaking only for defence.”
Attacks on Saudi Arabia
The request follows a barrage of attacks on the kingdom from Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, including airports and oil facilities.
Recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have mainly targeted key infrastructure on the outskirts of the capital, Riyadh, but they appear to be edging closer to the city centre.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport earlier this month killed 14 people and wounded more than 300. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports, including Dammam, Abha, Jazan and Najran.
Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government launched a full-scale military campaign against the Houthis this month to recapture territory seized by them.
El-Sisi had backed Saudi calls for secure and unhindered navigation in the Red Sea in a meeting with the Saudi Crown Prince, known as MBS, in Cairo last month.
A statement from the Egyptian presidency then said that “the security of Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states is an integral part of Egypt’s national security”.
Red Sea security
That meeting came just days after the Houthis seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast, gaining significant control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal.
Saudi Arabia already has a defence pact with Pakistan and Turkiye, known as the Mecca Alliance for Defence, which was signed in August.
Earlier this month, the three countries agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under the pact and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.
Analysts say Riyadh is looking for help to protect the kingdom and Red Sea shipping and that Egypt, whose Suez Canal revenue depends on the same traffic, is an obvious partner.
They say Egypt is eager to prevent Iran and its allies from imposing control over the region, especially over maritime traffic in the Red Sea, given the direct repercussions for the Suez Canal.
Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging Houthi attacks against the kingdom, a claim Tehran rejects. Iran has offered assistance to halt the conflict between the two sides.
Sisi’s future
Speaking to recruits at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital on Saturday, el-Sisi also confirmed that he would not seek to extend his presidency beyond 2030, in line with the Egyptian constitution.
“The period leading up to 2030 will be the end of my term as president of the state, if I am still alive,” he said.
He added that his decision is “completely settled” and there will be “no discussion” about it.
Egypt’s constitution was updated in 2019 to increase term length to six years from four, and to allow el-Sisi to run for another six-year term in 2023. That means his term is due to expire in 2030, and he is not allowed to run again.
He said the Egyptian constitution “would not be touched”.
